articles.title: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s rogue agents possibly tied to data service disruption in May
articles.summary: The Wikimedia Foundation says the disruption seemed to have been triggered as OpenAI agents visited millions of pages and made hundreds of thousands of data queries

blocks.text: OPENAI. The OpenAI logo and AI Artificial Intelligence words are seen in this illustration taken, May 4, 2023.
The Wikimedia Foundation says the disruption seemed to have been triggered as OpenAI agents visited millions of pages and made hundreds of thousands of data queries

WASHINGTON, USA – The Wikimedia Foundation, which operates online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said heavy traffic from OpenAI’s rogue agents was possibly tied to a disruption that its data service experienced in May.

In a blog post on Monday, October 5, Wikimedia said it could confirm “that we have discovered some activity by these ‘rogue’ OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms,” including a May incident that resulted in a “partial outage” of its Wikidata Query Service.
Wikimedia said the disruption seemed to have been triggered as the agents visited millions of pages and made hundreds of thousands of data queries.

Wikimedia also said the OpenAI agents made unauthorized edits to Wikimedia wiki sites, including “potentially malicious edits” to a citation tool, which the foundation said were likely intended to hijack it.
Wikimedia said its Etherpad note-taking tool was also hit by malicious activity from OpenAI’s agents.

OpenAI said in a statement that it appreciated Wikimedia’s “detailed findings” and was working with the organization to analyze the activity. “We’ll continue to share relevant information as that work progresses,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said.
OpenAI has been scrambling to get its arms around the full scope of its rogue agent activity, Reuters has previously reported. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sotto questions AMLC on bank glitch reducing Mans Carpio's transaction from P2B to P2M
articles.summary: Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked Tuesday if the glitch reported by a bank to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) involving transactions of Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:24pm

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked Tuesday if the glitch reported by a bank to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) involving transactions of Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, indeed happened
Sotto raised the question during his inquiry on AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, a prosecution witness who testified on the bank transactions of the Vice President and her husband.

Buenaventura testified that the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) asked that the covered and suspicious bank transactions involving Carpio be corrected, and that the AMLC did validation before granting BPI’s request for correction wherein the P2 billion bank transactions was changed to P2 million.

“Ang tagal tagal na panahon na meron akong account sa bangko. Ni minsan, hindi ako nakaranas nun, o may kakilala man lang na naging bilyon [ang pera] dahil sa bank system glitch. Nangyayari ba talaga ito na P2 billion naging P2 million?” Sotto said.
(I have been an account owner for so long. Not once that I or someone I know experienced a bank system glitch that big. Does that really happen, from P2 billion to P2 million?)

Buenaventura responded by saying that AMLC’s action on the matter was limited to validating BPI’s request for correction. He also clarified that such requests for correction from covered persons, including banks, happen and are subject to AMLC validation.

“BPI made a request, and we acted on the request by validating and conducting the necessary audit to confirm whether an error indeed occurred in the reporting and we found po that there is and we granted the request,” he said.

Buenaventura said that the BPI requested correction last April 8, 2026, which was days before his appointment, and that the validation of AMLC of the BPI’s request was not yet done when Buenaventura testified before the House justice panel hearing on the impeachment complaints against the Vice President.

The AMLC official also said that the documents he testified on before the Senate impeachment court on October 5 already reflected the BPI correction validated by the AMLC, reducing the amount of covered and suspicious transactions from P6.7 billion to P4.4 billion.
Still, Sotto pressed Buenaventura on whether a correction request from a covered person, such as banks like BPI, involving billions of bank transactions is a one-time event.
Buenaventura responded by saying the billions-level correction was a first under his tenure, but such requests for correction from banks happen.
“At least, from my time po as Executive Director, as far as I can recall po, this is thefirst po,” said Buenaventura, who was appointed as AMLC executive director on April 14, 2026.
“But we receive [requests for correction] on a regular po, sometimes may nagkakamali po talaga ng report, isa, dalawa po, then they request, and we validate,” he added. —AOL, GMA News

October 6, 2026
New Saxony-Anhalt parliament sits to choose speaker

blocks.caption: Tobias Rausch is poised to become the AfD's first speaker in a state parliamentImage: Marco Bader/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: The newly elected state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt is poised to hold its first session on Tuesday more than four weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won elections there with almost 44% of the vote.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the legislature, the same number of seats as the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) together.
During the session, parliamentarians are to vote for a speaker, with the AfD, as the strongest force, empowered to nominate the first candidate.
The AfD has put forward long-serving parliamentarian Tobias Rausch, 35, for the post, a choice that the populist BSW, which holds 5 seats, has pledged to back.
All the other parties refuse to work with the AfD under a policy known as the "firewall," and the CDU chairman in the state has advised members of his party to abstain from the vote.
If Rausch is elected, he will become the first AfD speaker of a state parliament in Germany.
However, if he fails to be elected in a first round of voting, all the other parties can put forward their own candidates.
There will be no vote on who will lead the state.

The session will be accompanied by protests by civil society groups who see the AfD, which has been classified as a "confirmed extremist" organization by domestic intelligence in the state, as a danger to Germany's democracy.

articles.title: OSG to SC: Extending barangay, SK term limits means lower polling costs
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Government lawyers have disputed the petition challenging the law postponing this year’s Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and extending the terms of office,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Government lawyers have disputed the petition challenging the law postponing this year’s Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and extending the terms of office, saying the postponement was grounded in governance and budget concerns.

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) on Monday filed its comment on the petition for certiorari filed by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal before the Supreme Court on Sept. 28. The OSG represented the respondents, namely the Office of the President, the Senate, the House of Representatives, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec).

This was in response to a directive by the high court last week for the respondents to comment on Macalintal’s petition, which challenged the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 12326. The law reset the BSKE, originally slated for Nov. 2 this year, to Nov. 13, 2028.

The new law also extended the term of office of barangay and SK officials to five years for up to two consecutive terms. This means an elected barangay or SK official may hold office for up to 10 straight years.
The OSG, in its comment, said that the Congress factored in “concrete governance reasons” for setting the five-year term.
Among them was that it would cut the cost of setting up polls, estimated at P19 billion per election, because a five-year term would mean fewer polls.
“A five-year term results in two elections over a ten-year period, as against three under a four-year term,” it pointed out.
A five-year term would also allow barangay and SK officials to complete projects that may take longer to execute, the OSG said.
“It affords the officials enough time to transition at the start of their term and refine their programs in the latter part of their term,” it added.

The government lawyers also noted that planning cycles are usually set at every five years, including the development plans required by the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Philippine Youth Development Plan.
Such reasons, among others, do not make RA 12326 unconstitutional, they stressed. /jpv

articles.title: Marcos headed to Singapore for working visit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is headed to Singapore for a working visit from October 7 to 11, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:01pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is headed to Singapore for a working visit from October 7 to 11, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Tuesday.
In a statement to the media, the DFA said Marcos was invited to Singapore by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

"Ang Working Visit na ito ay bahagi ng inisyatibo ng bansa upang mapalalim ang ating ugnayan sa Singapore, mapalawak ang ating economic engagement, at isulong ang ating kooperasyon sa mga sektor na makatutulong sa kaunlaran ng ating bansa," the statement read.

(This working visit is part of the country's initiative to deepen relations with Singapore, expand economic engagement, and to strengthen cooperation in sectors that would help progress in our country.)
The DFA also said the upcoming meet was important as the Philippines was about to end its chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and hand it over to Singapore.
Marcos is also set to attend the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference to meet with leading business leaders from Singapore and across the world.
This would allow the President to present investment opportunities in the Philippines, the DFA said.
"Bibisita rin ang Pangulo sa Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute, upang alamin ang karanasan at expertise ng Singapore sa nuclear technology and safety," the DFA said.
(The President will also visit the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute to learn more about the experience and expertise of Singapore in nuclear technology and safety.)

This will be Marcos' sixth trip to Singapore, following his visit last July where he also met with Wong to discuss matters related to the chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Marcos had also participated in the Milken Institute Private Roundtable Discussion in his last Singapore trip. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
articles.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.

blocks.text: OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June and said it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
Asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said, in response to a question by the committee on why it had not dialled the mobile numbers of government ministers.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators who are looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI".
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and an alarm was triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that it had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could means artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

articles.title: ‘Bully in every way’: domestic abuse survivors say ex-partners behind far-right UK street patrols
articles.summary:
Seven women share their stories to make people aware of patterns of violence behind anti-immigration street patrol movement

During their relationship, Lisa’s ex-partner was controlling. He…

blocks.text: During their relationship, Lisa’s ex-partner was controlling. He kept her at home where he was emotionally and physically abusive towards her, including once attacking her with a machete.

These days, he runs protests outside houses of multiple occupancy that he claims are housing asylum seekers. He coordinates groups of men to patrol the streets of his town, claiming to protect women but often using these patrols to profile and target men of colour.
“There’s nothing good about that man. He’s a bully in every way,” she says.

Lisa is one of seven women who have told the Guardian they are survivors of domestic abuse carried out by key figures in the anti-immigration street patrol movement. All have chosen to come forward to make the public aware of the patterns of violence behind this new form of activism.

At least 14 street patrol groups have been set up in towns and cities across the UK, receiving tens of thousands of pounds in public donations, as well as political support. The deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, has previously called for more patrols to take place.

Wearing hi-vis jackets and, in some cases, stab-proof vests and carrying handcuffs, these groups of men aim to be a visible presence conducting patrols through their towns and cities. Some have used their patrols to target men of colour, stopping and questioning individuals and demanding to see identity documents.

Despite using rhetoric of protecting women, the Guardian has been shown evidence that indicates the severity of the abuse carried out by men in these groups. Some of the women we have spoken to have been granted restraining or non-molestation orders. One was forced to move towns with the support of the police for her own safety.

“He likes power, and I feel like this is giving him some sort of power. It’s all about power and control in everything he does,” says Lisa, who met and began a relationship with a far-right activist when she was 16.

He is one of the main figures behind the branch of the Raising the Colours movement in his town. The far-right, anti-migrant campaign has hung flags from lamp-posts across the UK under the guise of “patriotism”.

Early in their relationship, Lisa’s partner became abusive and controlling, sometimes preventing her from leaving the house. This behaviour escalated after she became pregnant and had her first child. He would threaten her and her family if she attempted to end the relationship. “I still have nightmares to this day,” Lisa says.

The night that Lisa left him, he tried to attack her with a machete and gave her a black eye and several broken toes. Police attended the scene and arrested him but this was not the end of his abuse, Lisa says. “When I did get away, he was threatening me constantly. I had met somebody else eventually, and I was getting phone calls saying he’s going to kick the baby out of me when he sees me in the street.”
Despite the severity of this abuse, it never resulted in a conviction.

Claire was in a relationship with an anti-immigration activist for several years, during which she made various calls to the police due to his abusive and violent behaviour, which would often be carried out while her children were present.

He was verbally abusive to Claire while she was pregnant, as well as behaving aggressively towards hospital staff after the birth of their first child. This abuse continued after Claire’s pregnancy, including one occasion when he pulled Claire’s hair and gripped her by the throat.

He uses his elevated platform in the town to run street patrols, standing with men outside schools in the mornings and afternoons as children come and go, and erecting St George’s Cross flags on lamp-posts.
The Guardian previously revealed police data indicating patterns of intimate partner violence among 2024 rioters, and similar links can be observed for those involved in these forms of vigilantism.

blocks.caption: An anti-migrant protester faces a cordon of police at Gosport, Hampshire, on 22 September.  Photograph: Lab Mo/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Last August, Reece McCarron founded the Corby Guard, claiming he had been inspired to set up a group for the Northamptonshire town after seeing someone “making advances to a young girl on the way from school”. On early street patrols he was joined by James Kenna, who had a domestic violence protection order imposed on him in 2020.

A month later, McCarron broke into his former partner’s house, swinging a machete around the kitchen and threatening to kill her. He was later charged with a string of offences including rape, actual bodily harm and intentional strangulation, which have been dropped after support for prosecution was withdrawn by the victim. In May, he was convicted of coercive control, as the prosecutor told the courts “the victim said that she was very scared he would kill her. She couldn’t sleep for weeks.”
In Greater Manchester, Adam Farrell and Jamie Thomason formed the Heywood community guard. Several schools in Heywood were forced to go into lockdown when the guard ran patrols outside their gates.

Farrell was jailed in 2022 after a racist attack on a man that left him with life-changing brain injuries. Thomason has claimed he is “doing God’s work” protecting women and children. In 2018, he was convicted under section 4A of the Public Order Act after arriving at a former partner’s address, banging on her door, threatening to slit her throat and punching her car.
Names have been changed to protect the identity of the survivors of abuse.

articles.title: ‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms
articles.summary:
Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings

In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met…

blocks.text: In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week to plot their latest move: disrupting a tech industry dinner being addressed by a senior executive from the chip maker Nvidia.

Emma, a 28-year-old bartender, had never before taken direct action and was the most nervous of the four plotters from Pull The Plug, one of a growing number of AI-focused campaign groups around the world.

Around the table were a former climate protester and a campaigner versed in the anti-nuclear movement. Emma signed up after a summer of feeling rising alarm at the catastrophic risks of AI, first when a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website and then as Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit with an apocalyptic warning that superintelligent AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As darkness fell they crossed the Thames to the Claremont hotel where Emma filmed while two others unfurled a banner in a function room, shouting “Pull the plug on Nvidia” and “Pull the plug on Palantir”. Hundreds of protesters also staged a rally in front of Palantir’s London HQ last Thursday.

“We did not consent to the kind of build-out that you are planning here,” the activists yelled as they were wrestled out of the door. They edited a video clip – “activist disrupts elite AI network dinner – Nvidia edition” – and uploaded it to Instagram. It was a small gesture, but they had made their stand.

“I want to show other people that they don’t have to feel powerless among all of these articles coming out [about AI doom],” said Emma. “It’s easy to fall into a spiral that it’s too late. This shows people they can address the tech executives, disrupt their meetings, make them feel uncomfortable and get some answers.”

blocks.caption: A protest in London on 1 October against the AI firm Palantir, which has a series of UK government contracts. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

blocks.text: Pull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40. It is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the AI industry, organisers said. Several campaigns resisting AI acceleration are funded by tech insiders.

Pull The Plug advocates direct action – a tactic other AI campaigns have rejected. Last month, one of its members climbed on to a chair in a packed AI conference in London addressed by speakers from OpenAI and Amazon and delivered an impassioned speech.

“Best case scenario: the men handling this technology are completely incompetent,” the female activist said in an outburst that garnered 153,000 Instagram likes and was picked up by the Washington Post. “Worst case scenario: we are all being led into a disaster.”

Other AI protest movements are gaining momentum after a torrent of news about AI dangers. Anthropic told investors this week that advanced AI could pose “existential risks to humanity”. Pause AI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, saw a fourfold jump in sign-ups when worrying news about rogue AI agents was breaking in August and last month.

“We have had a lot of volunteers who have suddenly decided to dedicate way more of their time to the cause,” said Maxime Fournes, a Cambridge-educated mathematician and deep learning engineer who is chief executive of PauseAI Global. Volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and soared to 681 in the week of Coxon’s “kill us all” warning, when PauseAI organised protests in Paris, London and Berlin.

Donald Trump may be one of the movement’s most important recruiting sergeants. He announced last week that he wanted AI companies to “self-police” despite widespread demands, including from the companies, for federal and international rules to limit AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.

The surge in worrying news has given campaigners like Fournes hope that “we could actually survive this situation”. He added: “Suddenly we have a large fraction of the world population that is waking up.”

Joseph Miller, an AI safety researcher who has suspended his doctoral studies at Oxford University to run Pause AI’s UK branch, noticed the shift while campaigning outside Brixton tube station in London. He said: “It was the easiest flyering we’ve ever done, because people would just come and talk to me … one every few minutes.”
People he spoke to were worried about cognitive decline in schools and AI resulting in sloppy work in the office. “I heard ‘killing everyone’ more from young people,” Miller added.

Pausing or halting AI is a cause that cuts across political and generational boundaries, according to campaigners. University students sign up because they fear AI will wreck career paths, while older conservationists rally against datacentre construction.
after newsletter promotion

In Scotland, where at least 21 datacentres are planned, Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a 100-year old charity better known for campaigning for green belt land, said its supporter list had swollen from 400 to 4,000.

“I’ve never seen grassroots energy like this,” said Kat Jones, the charity’s director. She affectionately calls it “a campaign of nerds” with supporters probing the workings of AI datacentre cooling systems and the power grid and lodging freedom of information requests.

AI’s need for vast physical infrastructure has provided a “very physical, concrete object of protest”, said Fournes, and, in some cases, a target for direct action. In the last year, far-left or anarchist groups protesting over the climate crisis and AI have claimed responsibility for criminal attacks on infrastructure in France and Germany.

In August, Wynd Kaufmyn, became the first anti-AI protester believed to have been jailed for taking direct action – in her case blocking the entrance to OpenAI’s HQ in San Francisco. In April, another protester hurled a petrol bomb at the house of the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman. The same month, an attacker fired gunshots into the home of an Indianapolis politician in protest at datacentre plans.

Mauro Lubrano, assistant professor of terrorism and political violence at the University of Leiden, said that if rising demands for accountability, transparency, and democracy in AI governance were not met, more people could get drawn to violence.

“It’s quite likely that we will see anti-AI violence becoming more prominent as a driver to political violence,” he said, citing last month’s vandalism of a Canadian AI institute, Mila, and a nearby software company in Montreal. Windows were smashed and graffiti scrawled reading “burn the data centers”.

Some Pull The Plug activists have diverted their energy from Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. One member of Emma’s cell glued herself to roads to protest against the climate crisis – tactics that have alienated the public.

Such direct action is “extremely counterproductive”, said Fournes who predicted it would trigger “an immune response” from wider society and would provide “a golden opportunity for the AI labs … to say, they are criminals and it is easier to turn the broader public against the movement against the development of AI”.
Whatever the tactics, a movement is stirring.

articles.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
articles.summary:
Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year.

Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index.

The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April.
But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s.
That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points.
Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s.
“Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said.
“The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.”
Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected.

Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded.
AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices.
“On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said.

“The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.”
Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points.
Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month.
Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points.
Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong.
Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Why the Green party’s Zionism vote has caused a backlash
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The party has voted to define Zionism as racist and back a single Palestinian state. But what does the policy mean, why has it caused alarm among Jewish members, and how…

blocks.text: Good morning.

The Green party of England and Wales is in turmoil. Following a vote to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism, and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”, some Jewish members say they are considering whether they are welcome in the party.

While Green members celebrated, or mourned, the motion passing, some have questioned its purpose, arguing it will distract from what’s important – keeping eyes on Gaza and holding the Israeli government to account – instead igniting a divisive discussion about ideology that will only harm the party.

Today, I spoke to Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland, to understand how the vote has been received by many Jewish people beyond the Greens, and senior political correspondent Peter Walker, who reported on the fallout of the vote at the party conference in Brighton at the weekend. That’s after the headlines …
Five big stories

items: RAF Fairford | No 10 has insisted the Gloucestershire base is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers that had been stationed there amid security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.
Donald Trump | Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%.
Brazilian elections | Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, is poised to win the Brazilian presidency, after a shock first-round victory.
Jeffrey Archer | Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86.

Cancer | Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.

blocks.text: In depth: Why the Greens are divided over Zionism

blocks.caption: Green party leader Zack Polanski faces questions over the Greens’ new position on Zionism. Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/Alamy

blocks.text: Yesterday, the head of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein confirmed that she is considering leaving the party after Sunday’s vote. Many other Jewish Greens – a significant majority of whom described themselves as anti-Zionists when polled – are similarly taking stock.

Much of the fallout was predictable. The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and Israel immediately barred Zack Polanski, the Green party’s Jewish leader, from entering the country. The Israeli foreign ministry denounced the motion as “a stain on the history of the United Kingdom”.

With four of the Green’s five MPs opposing the new policy, yesterday evening the group representing European Green parties expressed dismay at the move which runs counter to their support for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. There is now growing anger internally with Polanski, who avoided the debate to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where he is running for former prime minister Keir Starmer’s seat.
What is the motion about – and who supports it?

Zionism isn’t a clearly defined, singular ideology. Broadly speaking, it means support for Jewish self-determination, realised today in the state of Israel. The motion argues that Zionism is racist because it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others” and that in Israel this is based upon “European settler-colonial systems of domination and oppression”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism … and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists”.

Prior to this, senior Greens have been some of the most vehement voices in the UK in condemning Israel’s destruction of Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry found to be a genocide. They have also spoken out against the ongoing occupation of the West Bank, as well as pushing for a full arms and trade embargo.

The motion was put forward by Greens for Palestine, an internal pressure group that calls for the creation of a single Palestinian state, in which Jews and Palestinians can freely live. There is clearly broad support for this general principle – the motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813. One of the sponsors, Kieran Andrieu, a British Palestinian, described it as a “unifying motion”, arguing there was “enormous virtue” in naming what he said was a “damaging ideology”. During the debate, he added, “everyone was agreeing that we need to disagree agreeably”.

The vote happened behind closed doors, but longstanding Green supporters have shared with Peter their concerns that the motion was being pushed by relatively new members. Greens for Palestine have been very open about encouraging people to join the party to support this single issue.
The reaction

A legal case against the new policy is highly likely – some Green members are already consulting lawyers over whether the party could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation. Barrister Adam Wagner KC, who led a case that decided Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party broke equalities laws over antisemitism, told Peter he believed such a case would have a good chance of success.

There is huge frustration, particularly from longer established members, at what they consider a lack of leadership from Polanski. First, in trying to cancel the conference to free up his supporters to campaign for him, and second for missing the debate on a hugely divisive matter. Other senior party figures, such as the former co-leader Carla Denyer, have voiced concern that the motion draws attention away from what’s important.

“I’m concerned that elected Greens will be forced to spend our time and energy debating and defending definitions, at the expense of focusing on the essential actions that only we can take to make things materially better for people in Palestine,” Denyer said in a statement on X.

Polanski has said he agrees that Zionism, when defined as “the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people”, does “clearly” constitute racism. Critics say he could have supported what was regarded as a “safeguarding” amendment, which offered reassurance that members would not be disciplined for their membership of Jewish organisations with Zionist affiliations, even synagogues – as the amendment did not garner enough support to pass.

This is a now a “genuine fear” among some Jewish members, Peter tells me. Greens for Palestine have consistently stated this was not its intention, emphasising that the policy refers to Zionism as a political ideology, supporting the state of Israel which they believe relies on apartheid and racism to uphold a majority Jewish population.

“But as the Jewish Greens pointed out, Zionism can mean so many different things,” said Peter. A Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza, a left-leaning kibbutznick and a Netanyahu supporter will each have different interpretations. “Many now worry that this enshrines a definition of Zionism that only reflects an extreme, right wing version of it.”
What is Zionism, and who identifies with it?

“To brand everyone under that one umbrella as a racist shows a deep ignorance of what the word Zionism means and the sheer range of people who identify with it,” is the point Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland made ahead of the Green conference vote.

When we spoke yesterday, he told me that the motion’s success marked “a shift in the Overton window” that has left many people well beyond Green party activists alarmed: “A mainstream political party has adopted a position, which functionally identifies most British Jews as racists,” he suggests.

Jonathan references the celebrated Israeli writer and peace activist Amos Oz, who described Zionism as a ‘family name’. “‘Zionist’ alone doesn’t tell you much. You need to have a first name to make sense of it: whether that’s socialist Zionism, Marxist-Zionism, religious Zionism or cultural Zionism,” he says.

There are non-Zionist and anti-Zionist Jews, too. Many of those Jewish activists defending Palestinians from settler violence on the West Bank, he explains, would describe themselves as Zionists – just as extremist settlers would.

For many British Jews – nearly two-thirds of whom identify as Zionist according to a report by the Institute for Jewish Policy Research published on Monday – this is not about support for Israeli government policy, current or past. “For many Jews, when you use the term Zionism rather than Israel, you’re in the realm of a dream or an aspiration; one that is a constitutive part of the Jewish identity,” he says.
It’s an outlook informed by generations of persecution, which is one reason why the comparison to ‘settler-colonialism’ that the Green motion makes is anathema to so many, he adds.

The mood is also reflected in the research, which also found British Jews have become more likely to identify as Zionist, consider emigrating to Israel, or feel a close attachment to the country since the 7 October attacks.

Meanwhile, younger Jewish people, aged sixteen- to 29-year-olds were less likely to say Israel was “very important” to their identity, with the percentage falling by one point – to 27% – in 2024. This aligns with some Jewish commentators who argue there is a generational shift in the Jewish diaspora, with those younger people appalled by Israel’s actions in Gaza identifying less as Zionist than their parents’ generation.
What could it mean for the Greens?

Most close observers believe that the Zionism motion is unlikely to make a difference to the outcome of Thursday’s byelection: Labour are very confident of transforming Starmer’s base and Burnham’s bounce into a win, while Polanksi himself has rolled the pitch in advance, saying it’s a 50/50 outcome that won’t impact his authority as leader.
after newsletter promotion

The longer term problem for the party, Peter argues, is that this one policy dispute overshadows all others, and might even cap Green support at a point when the party was on the cusp of an electoral breakthrough.

“On Sunday, after the Zionism vote, they announced a series of key economic policies that no one paid any attention to. This is all they’re going to be able to talk about, maybe up to the next election, and voters don’t like parties that look like they are mired in chaos,” he says.

articles.title: Accenture contractor removed from FBI following damaging data breach, sources say
articles.summary: The breach triggers concern across the FBI and the wider intelligence community

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, USA – The Federal Bureau of Investigation removed an Accenture contractor on Monday, October 5, over their role in a damaging data breach that exposed sensitive personal details of thousands of bureau employees, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The development comes as the FBI is still trying to ascertain the ramifications of the breach, which some former bureau officials have described as a major blow to the organization’s operational security.
In a statement to Reuters, a senior FBI official confirmed that an unidentified contractor had failed to properly update — or patch — the system they were responsible for.

“To date, our review has determined that the incident occurred as the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform,” FBI cyber chief Brett Leatherman said in the statement. “As such, the FBI has removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce.”

The FBI did not identify the platform or third-party organization, but the two sources familiar with the matter said the platform was Oracle’s PeopleSoft, a human resources platform that the hacking group ShinyHunters said it exploited to break into the FBI’s job site last month.
Oracle did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
The sources also said the third-party organization was Accenture. Reuters could not immediately identify the specific contractor or determine their current employment status.
In a statement, Accenture said it was “proud to support the mission of the FBI and will continue to do so.” It did not answer questions about the contractor or their alleged failure to patch.

In June, Google raised the alarm over a ShinyHunters-linked hack-and-extort campaign aimed at organizations using PeopleSoft ‌software. The same day, Oracle issued a security alert identifying a weakness in PeopleSoft and offering security fixes.
Both companies urged organizations running PeopleSoft to “apply all Critical Patch Updates, Critical Security Patch Updates and Security Alerts without delay.”

Swift patching of vulnerable software is considered a key part of defending networks and devices against hackers, but the process can be laborious and difficult, particularly with enterprise software that serves large numbers of people.

Reuters has not been able to determine whether or when those responsible for securing the FBI’s job site followed those recommendations, but ShinyHunters credited a vulnerability in PeopleSoft for facilitating its intrusion.

The breach has triggered concern across the FBI and the wider intelligence community, exposing sensitive personal information, including granular descriptions of named employees’ counterintelligence jobs, street addresses of human intelligence operatives, and medical and psychiatric records of bureau workers.

Last week, a key ShinyHunters suspect was detained in Jordan, Reuters reported. Sources told Reuters the alleged hacker was cooperating, a development that may help the bureau limit — or at the very least understand — the scope of the damage.

articles.title: P9.06-B farm-to-market road program to cover 5 Luzon regions
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) have signed a memorandum of agreement for P9.06 billion worth of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects covering…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 1:07pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) have signed a memorandum of agreement for P9.06 billion worth of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects covering five regions in Luzon.

The program will cover 605 FMR projects with a combined length of 604 kilometers in the Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and the Cordillera Administrative Region, the DA said.

“The government also employs infrastructure monitoring mechanisms and a digital portal to track project implementation and project status as the road program moves from planning to construction,” the DA said in a statement.
“Beyond moving farm products, improved roads can connect producers to traders, processors, and consumers while enhancing access to services and economic opportunities in rural communities,” it added.
The P9.06-billion program translates to an average cost of about P15 million per kilometer.
The new road projects come as the proposed P198.45-billion budget for the DA in 2027 includes P16 billion for FMR projects, half of the P33 billion allocation for the program in the 2026 budget.
The Department of Agrarian Reform earlier said 537 FMR projects had been completed since the start of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s administration in 2022.
The completed projects cover a total distance of 435.807 kilometers and supposedly benefit 155,123 agrarian reform beneficiaries.— MCG, GMA News

October 6, 2026
INDIA bloc to hold protest march to Election Commission against chief Gyanesh Kumar

Leaders and MPs from India's opposition parties are set to carry out a protest march to the Election Commission of India's (ECI) headquarters in New Delhi on Tuesday as they call for the sacking of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over controversial voter list changes.
Security arrangements have been beefed up around the national poll body's headquarters, media reports said Tuesday morning.

The INDIA bloc — the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties — announced the march last week as part of a broader 'Save Democracy' campaign under which its leaders have been holding demonstrations since October 2 over alleged irregularities made by the ECI.
The opposition is demanding the removal of Kumar, who is facing allegations of taking unilateral action in connection with mass culling of names from registered voter lists.

Critics say the action, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters by removing their names from voter lists and that the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The ECI and the BJP reject the allegations.
Around 130 million names have been removed from electoral rolls since the changes began last year.
The opposition march on Tuesday will begin from Parliament House.
INDIA bloc leaders are later also expected to meet President Droupadi Murmu to raise concerns over the SIR exercise, reports said.

articles.title: Agreement to transition away from fossil fuels ‘not open for renegotiation’, Pacific leader tells pre-Cop
articles.summary:
International leaders visit Tuvalu as part of climate talks co-hosted by Australia ahead of Cop31 conference

Pacific island leaders have urged a promised global transition away from fossil…

blocks.text: Pacific island leaders have urged a promised global transition away from fossil fuels must not be left open to renegotiation as they gather in tiny Tuvalu in a bid to build momentum before a major climate summit.

About 50 dignitaries – 14 national heads including Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, a list of climate change ministers and the heads of global agencies – flew to the low-lying atoll nation in a bid to bring attention to the plight of the countries most at risk from the climate crisis.

As a showcase for the remote Pacific promised by Albanese, things could have gone more smoothly. Tuvalu was wet and grey, and the capital of Funafuti – spectacular from the air on a clear day – was visible only in strips between heavy rain clouds during descent.

The visit was promised by the Albanese government last year as part of a compromise deal when it missed out on hosting the Cop31 conference. The event will be in Turkey next month; the Pacific is hosting a preparatory meeting, mostly in Fiji.

Speaking at a “saultalaga” – an exchange of views around a meeting table – at the end of a three-hour visit, a string of leaders argued the world must stand behind a 2023 agreement, made at a UN summit in Dubai, to transition away from fossil fuels. More recently it has faced wavering support, with pushback particularly led by oil-producing nations.

Tuvalu is among a handful of countries most at risk from the climate crisis. A collection of three reef islands and six atolls, it is mostly less than 2 metres above sea level. About half its population of 10,600 live in a corner of Funafuti.

The visitors heard from Melelusi Sokotia, a 13-year-old local student. She said her friends dreamed of “becoming teachers, doctors, builders” but spent their lives wondering if their island would be safe to live on when they were adults. “We all have one single dream: to grow safely here in Tuvalu,” she said. “We are not asking for peace. We are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”

The Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said with the world on the brink of overshooting the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C – agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and facing a super El Niño, it must bring forward plans to cut emissions. “That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation, and the scientific reality,” he said. “The transition away from fossil fuels was agreed to by all of us in Dubai. It is not a new ask, and it is not open for renegotiation.”

Tuvalu’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, stressed island states needed faster access to global climate funding to deal with worsening extreme events. “Why should countries like Tuvalu take on more debt to protect ourselves from a climate crisis we did so little to cause? We should not have to borrow our way out of a crisis.”

The visit came less than a week after an Australian state regulator approved the latest of more than 30 fossil fuel developments to have been given the greenlight in the country in less than five years.

Albanese, attending his first UN climate conference as prime minister since his election in 2022, said the message from the Tuvalu trip was that “climate change must be understood as being something more than about science or targets”.
after newsletter promotion

“It must be understood that effectively it’s about people, is what it comes down to,” he said. “And the impact on humanity. The perspective of elders reminds us of what must be protected – the knowledge, the identity, the traditions and the culture pass from one generation to the next.”

After being greeted by a cultural ceremony, the leaders were shown a land reclamation project to extend space for homes and infrastructure by about 20 hectares using sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon inside the atoll. Overseen by the UN Development Program and partly funded by the Australian government, the project is a race against time.

Tuvalu’s director of climate change, Jamie Ovia, said the flooding risk was worsening, with the likelihood of what was once a 100-year flood increasing as the sea level rose. Projected sea level rise this century could increase the annual economic damage from flooding and storm surges to US$34m a year by 2050 and $63m – more than Tuvalu’s GDP – by 2100.
He said the coastal fishing catch could be cut by 16% and tuna stocks worth $4m a year to the local economy could be lost as the seas warmed and species moved away from the atoll nation.
“We need time to adapt,” Ovia said. “Tuvalu is doing our part. Will you act with Tuvalu and will you act in time?”

articles.title: UK regulator FCA to investigate how it handled Epstein whistleblower who took his own life
articles.summary:
British banker Simon Andriesz helped to expose alleged ties between late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick

A top UK regulator has launched an…

blocks.text: A top UK regulator has launched an investigation into how it handled a whistleblower – who highlighted alleged ties between the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick – after he took his own life.
The British banker Simon Andriesz died late last month aged 57, the campaign group Transparency Task Force, of which he was a member, confirmed over the weekend.

Andriesz had formerly worked as a managing director at BGC Group, the financial brokerage where Lutnick had been chief executive. He had accused the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of failing to hold his former employer to account for alleged wrongdoing, and had been wrongly told he did not qualify for whistleblower protection.

blocks.caption: The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

blocks.text: The banker had spent years raising concerns about his former employer: first in regards to accounting irregularities – which he raised internally at BGC in 2016, a year before he was sacked – and then in 2020-21, when he reportedly told the FBI that Lutnick had undeclared business ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Lutnick has since said he had no “personal or professional relationship” with Epstein.

Andriesz, who had been living in Cornwall, later unearthed an email chain in the Epstein files that suggested Lutnick and Epstein had discussed the prospects of a startup business they were both involved in, in 2018. Epstein died in jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

However, Andriesz told the BBC’s File on 4 Investigates this summer that authorities in the US and UK had failed to hold BGC and its parent company, Cantor Fitzgerald, properly to account, or protect him from potential retaliation. He also later accused the FCA of mistreating whistleblowers, and raised concerns about the toll that whistleblowing had taken on his family, career and health.

The FCA had also given Andriesz misleading information, saying he would not qualify for whistleblower protection because his identity had become known. The regulator apologised to him and said that further guidance and training would be provided to its whistleblowing team.

The FCA confirmed it had now tasked a new board member to investigate how staff handled Andriesz’s concerns. “We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz’s death,” an FCA spokesperson said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends. Since expressing our condolences, we’d asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future.”

However, the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on investment fraud and fairer financial services is concerned that the FCA is being allowed to “mark its own homework” and called on the regulator to pay an independent party to “forensically and objectively evaluate its handling of whistleblowers”.

The APPG’s chair, the Labour MP John McDonnell, said: “It is vital that this time a truly independent and non-conflicted organisation carries out the work needed. If the FCA refuses to respond positively, the APPG will consider all alternatives, including conducting its own call for evidence from whistleblowers who have interacted with the regulator.”

Lutnick has not been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and has previously said: “I unequivocally condemn the conduct attributed to Jeffrey Epstein and everyone who participated in his illegal activities. The survivors of his crimes deserve our respect and support.”

A BGC spokesperson said: “BGC has long disputed Mr Andriesz’s allegations but does not intend to relitigate these matters at this sad time. BGC is sorry to hear this tragic news and expresses our condolences to Mr Andriesz’s family.”

articles.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
articles.summary:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern…

blocks.text: As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.
Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.
Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.
“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.
“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

blocks.caption: Members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in the regional capital, Mekelle, last month after TPLF rebels seized the city’s airport. Ethiopian forces later retook it. Photograph: AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”
Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.
Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

articles.title: Buenaventura: AMLC didn't rectify records submitted to impeachment court
articles.summary: Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura on Tuesday said there were no rectifications made to the records they already submitted to the Senate impeachment court.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 12:53pm
Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura on Tuesday said there were no rectifications made to the records they already submitted to the Senate impeachment court.
Buenaventura, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, said this on the 34th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
“Your Honor, we did not rectify the records that we submitted. The records, when we were subpoenaed here, have already been corrected based on our validation,” he said.

“So, it was not rectified because there was nothing at the time that we submitted our records, submitted before the House. When we were subpoenaed, these were the records standing in our database. Now, there was a request. We validated that,” he added.
During Monday’s trial, Buenaventura said P4.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions were recorded under the bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.
But this was far from what the AMLC presented during the April 22 hearing, wherein transactions totaling P6.7 billion—classified as covered and suspicious—were recorded under the couple’s names.

The camp of Carpio earlier said that the reported P2 billion total inflow into his bank for two decades, as reported before the House Committee on Justice's impeachment hearing, should only be P2 million.
Carpio’s camp said "a systems glitch" at the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) supposedly caused the discrepancy.
According to Buenaventura, when the BPI made the request to rectify, the AMLC still had to make a validation.

“So at that time, the records stood as it was because we have not yet validated. They simply sent a letter. When we submitted to this Honorable Court for transparency, Your Honor, it is already what is already as corrected based on the request because we have validated that,” he explained.

“So we never rectified anything because there was no error in the first place when we submitted before the House, and at this point because it's the covered person which made that request. And as of the time, we haven't yet validated that,” he continued.

In a statement in May, BPI said, “As a Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP)-supervised institution, Bank of the Philippine Islands adheres strictly to all applicable laws and regulations, including those governing bank secrecy, data privacy, and consumer protection."
BPI also said it “complies with required reporting and regulatory engagements through the proper authorities, and provides relevant clarifications when necessary.” — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte: Gracioso is motivated by money
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday belied claims by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered cash to her, saying the latter is motivated by money and resentment towards former…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 12:43pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday belied claims by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered cash to her, saying the latter is motivated by money and resentment towards former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his family.
“Ang motibo niya ay sama ng loob sa mga Velasco at pera (His motive is resentment toward the Velascos and money),” she said in a press briefing.

To recall, Gracioso previously alleged that he delivered cash to the Vice President, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, and forrmer President Rodrigo Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.
Duterte presented a screenshot of her conversation with Velasco, where she sent him a screenshot of Gracioso’s affidavit and asked him who he was.
Velasco replied that Gracioso was his former security aide.

Duterte said the former House speaker told her that Gracioso was given cash to campaign for a party-list in Samar. Velasco also told Duterte that Gracioso asked for cash for hospital bills and medicine.
The Vice President said Velasco told her that his wife, Rowena, told Gracioso that they will handle everything. However, Gracioso refused and said he wanted them to send cash.
Duterte said she did not ask Velasco’s permission that she will screenshot the message and reveal it to the public.
“May mga pahayag sa affidavit ni Gracioso at sa mensaheng pinadala sa akin ni Lord na na nagpapakitang nagkaroon sila ng hindi pagkakaunawaan kaugnay sa pera,” she said.
(There are statements in Gracioso’s affidavit and in the message sent to me by Lord that show they had a disagreement regarding money.)

“Ano man ang naging problema o hindi pagkakaunawan ni Lord at Gracioso, hindi ako dapat idadamay sa kanilang personal na alitan sa pera. Hindi dapat gamitin ang aking pangalan sa paghihiganti sa mga kasinungalingan at pagpapalakas ng walang ebidensya na impeachment complaint at sa paninira sa pulitika,” she added.

(Whatever problem or misunderstanding Lord and Gracioso had, I should not be dragged into their personal dispute over money. My name should not be used for retaliation through lies and for strengthening an impeachment complaint without evidence and for political attacks.)
Duterte also said she believes that Gracioso has nothing against her.
Velasco’s camp previously said the allegations against him had “no basis.” —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: NSC to probe alleged China money sent to Sara Duterte-linked firm
articles.summary: The National Security Council (NSC) on Tuesday said it would look into alleged financial inflows from China into a company linked to the family of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 12:39pm
The National Security Council (NSC) on Tuesday said it would look into alleged financial inflows from China into a company linked to the family of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In a statement, National Security Adviser Secretary Eduardo Oban Jr. said the NSC is taking seriously the related developments presented during the ongoing impeachment trial of the Vice President.

"The NSC takes seriously the information presented during the impeachment proceedings regarding reported financial inflows from China into a Philippine-based company associated with the family of Vice President Sara Duterte," Oban said.
He noted that information presented during the proceedings must first be properly examined through established legal processes.

Oban said the reported transactions involving significant foreign financial flows and any credible information that could have implications for national security warrant a "careful, in-depth, and responsible assessment."

"The NSC will look into the information presented and, as a matter of policy, continue to task the intelligence and investigative agencies and coordinate with relevant government institutions to assess the national security implications, if any, arising from the reported transactions," he said.

In his testimony on Day 33 of the trial, Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, who was considered to stand as a prosecution witness in the impeachment trial, claimed in a press conference on Friday that the Duterte couple accepted P150 million and P319 million through their separate organizations.

Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro has urged Trillanes to submit evidence regarding his claims so these could be "thoroughly investigated," saying these "raise serious implications for national security."
Over the weekend, the vice president's spokesperson Atty. Paolo Panelo said accusations that Duterte has links to China because she allegedly received funds from the Chinese are without basis.

Panelo said, "May donation ng Chinese government sa Tapang at Malasakit [Foundation], and the Vice President is one of the trustees. Awtomatikong agad na sinusuportahan ng Chinese government si Vice President?"

(There is a donation by the Chinese government to the Tapang at Malasakit Foundation, and the Vice President is one of the trustees. The Chinese government is automatically supporting the Vice President.)
"What if it was used to build classrooms? Or what if it was used for charitable purposes at may resibo (Or what if it was used for charitable purposes and there is a receipt)?" he added.

Also on Monday, the Chinese Embassy in Manila branded as a "false narrative" the allegations that China funneled funds to a political faction in the Philippines, calling these "malicious rhetoric and actions."

The embassy did not name any Philippine party, but urged "relevant individuals in the Philippines to stop political manipulation and not to drag Philippine domestic politics into China-Philippines relations." — VDV, GMA News

blocks.text: AFP SAYS
Published October 6, 2026 12:30pm
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) on Tuesday said a total of 101 Chinese vessels have been monitored in some West Philippine Sea (WPS) features in September 2026.
This was higher compared to the 56 Chinese ships seen in the disputed area in August 2026.

In an update, AFP spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and China Coast Guard (CCG) vessels were seen in WPS features from September 1 to 30:
• Ayungin Shoal – 14 CCGs, nine PLANs
• Bajo de Masinloc – 25 CCGs, 14 PLANs
• Escoda Shoal – seven CCGs, four PLANs
• Pag-asa Islands – 23 CCGs, five PLANs

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: RSPCA NSW director quits over welfare standards for RSPCA-branded chicken
articles.summary:
Mark Steele says he is ‘ashamed to be associated’ with the RSPCA Certified scheme, which badges 97% of chicken sold in Australia

  • Get our

blocks.text: RSPCA New South Wales’s vice-president has left the animal welfare group, saying he is “sincerely ashamed” of the standards for RSPCA-certified chicken.

Mark Steele, a senior counsel who was a volunteer member of the board from 2021 also served as a non-executive director of RSPCA Australia until March, issued a statement on LinkedIn outlining his decision to leave the group’s NSW branch for good at the end of September.

“The RSPCA does much fine work,” he wrote. “But there is one thing I have long been ashamed to be associated with: the use of the RSPCA’s trusted brand, through the RSPCA Certified scheme, to certify the welfare of 97% of Australia meat chicken.”
Chicken accounts for almost half of all meat eaten in Australia. Consumption has doubled in the past 30 years, and Australians now eat an average of about 55kg of chicken meat per person per year.

Almost all of the 800 million chickens slaughtered for meat in Australia each year are from one of two fast-growing breeds, which reach slaughter weight at between four and six weeks of age. Animal welfare experts say this rapid growth can stress the animals’ bodies.
Most chicken produced in Australia is also RSPCA Certified, a badge which signals to consumers that the product meets higher welfare standards.

“In my view, a shopper who sees that RSPCA logo would naturally assume – and ought to be entitled to assume – that the bird lived a good life and died a humane death,” Steele wrote. “In my opinion, a life like that cannot fairly be called good; which is why I don’t buy this chicken.”

Jed Goodfellow, the director of policy and government relations at Australian Alliance for Animals, said meat chickens grown that quickly can experience a range of issues, including cardiovascular, skeletal and dermatological problems “as their biology is pushed to the limits”.

“Healthier slower growing breeds are now being used in many parts of the world, particularly Europe … It may cost slightly more, but as their experience shows, the increase is not prohibitive, as European consumers increasingly opt for the healthier option,” he said.

Steele’s post comes just weeks after the RSPCA upgraded its animal welfare standards for chicken meat, which must be enacted by 1 January 2031 for producers to maintain their certification. Those changes include lower stocking densities, variable light intensity in sheds, and the phasing out of a slaughtering method called electrical water bath stunning.

But the new standards do not include phasing out fast-growing breeds. Instead, the organisation announced a new category of “enhanced” welfare standards which encourage producers to switch to slower-growing chicken breeds. The enhanced category does not yet have a label for consumers to identify, and those standards are voluntary.
after newsletter promotion
Steele said the new standards were a “small step forward” but criticised both the opt-in encouragement to adopt slower-growing breeds and the lack of an end date to phase out fast-growing breeds.

He said consumers would not recognise the welfare issue with fast-growing breeds “while the most trusted name in Australian animal welfare sits on the packaging, answering the question before the shopper has even thought to ask it”.
“Until it does, I will remain sincerely ashamed that the name of an organisation I otherwise love and respect appears on this chicken.”
Last month, the RSPCA’s senior scientific officer, Melina Tensen, told Guardian Australia the organisation would ultimately like to see slower-growing breeds replace fast-growing breeds.
“We definitely encourage consumers to be vocal about supporting this transition … because every dollar you spend is a message to the retailer,” she said.
