articles.title: Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international study finds
articles.summary:
Researchers, who looked at UK, US and Dutch data, say lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives a year

Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in…
articles.byline: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent

blocks.text: Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.
The number of people under 50 diagnosed with prostate cancer in England has quadrupled since 2001, while early onset bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses more than doubled.

Analysis of English, US and Dutch cancer data by World Cancer Research Fund identified “significant increases” in early onset cancers for seven cancer types in England, five types in the US and four in the Netherlands.
Although cancer has been increasing across all age groups globally, the rate rise in early onset cases is greater than other ages.
Experts said the figures reflected the growing global obesity epidemic, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as growing awareness of cancer and earlier diagnosis.
Cancer among the under 50s is still uncommon, with the median age at diagnosis above 60, but the trend is worrying, the authors noted.

Mark Lawler, professor of digital health and the chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, called the problem “a ticking timebomb that we need to diffuse as quickly as possible, otherwise the numbers will undoubtedly continue to grow”.
He went on: “The overall trend is also particularly worrying as it comes on the backdrop of lifestyle factors contributing to thousands of deaths.”

In England, of the 12 tumour types studied, incidence rates of prostate cancer among men under 50 jumped from one in every 100,000 people in 2001 to 3.6 in every 100,000 in 2023. Over the same period, rates of bowel cancer among the under 50s leapt from 3.9 in 100,000 people in 2001 to 8.4 in 100,000 in 2023, while early onset uterine and kidney cancers also doubled to 3.9 and 3 per 100,000 people respectively.

The rate of breast cancer among the under 50s increased, albeit less sharply, from 42 to 47.5 per 100,000 in 2023, while there were also increases in the incidence of early onset pancreatic and liver cancers.

In the US, analysis of official data since 2000 found that among patients under 50, incidence rates of kidney cancer more than doubled from 2.5 in 100,000 people in 2000 to 5.3 in 2023, while bowel, uterine and pancreatic cancers all increased by more than 50% and breast cancer by about 20%.
For the Netherlands, the researchers found significant increases in early onset bowel, kidney, liver and cervical cancers.
In contrast, rates of lung cancer among the under 50s declined in all three countries, reflecting continuing declines in smoking in those countries.

Dr Giota Mitrou, the executive director of research and policy at the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), called the trajectory “concerning”, and added: “Behind every figure is a person facing cancer earlier than they, their family and often their doctor would expect. While cancer is still much more common in older adults, these changing patterns among younger generations need to be treated as a serious research and cancer prevention priority.”

WCRF said risk factors such as growing obesity levels, poor diet, insufficient exercise, alcohol consumption, smoking and environmental exposures (such as pollutants, chemicals, plastics, water and air pollution) could be contributing to the trend. About 40% of cancers are linked to these kinds of modifiable risks. However, greater awareness of cancer symptoms also means that people are more likely to be diagnosed earlier.
after newsletter promotion

“While we don’t completely understand why more cancers are occurring in people under 50 years of age, it is likely that risk factors related to cancer – for example, overweight and obesity, diet, alcohol, consumption and smoking – play a role,” said Dr Vanessa Gordon-Dseagu, research translation manager at WCRF.

“At the same time, the public are increasingly aware of the risk factors relating to cancer and the signs and symptoms of the disease to look out for, so are more likely to seek out healthcare when they experience them.”
While more cancers are being diagnosed at an earlier stage, “increased diagnosis does not explain the whole story and more research is needed to understand early-onset cancers” she added.
King’s College London has announced a new trial of 250,000 people, funded by Cancer Research UK, to investigate the increase in bowel cancer cases among younger adults.
The study will seek a clearer understanding of the balance between worsening risk factors and better detection in the rise.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “These findings underline why early diagnosis is at the heart of our national cancer plan. To help catch cancer sooner, we’re investing in new technologies to speed up diagnosis, expanding genetic testing, and supporting research to better understand the causes of cancer and who may be most at risk.

We’re also prioritising research into less-survivable and rarer cancers, and our ambition is for three-quarters of people diagnosed by 2035 to be cancer-free or living well with cancer, saving 320,000 lives.
“Our newly announced national cancer board has a specific representative for children and young people, as we’re aware of the devastating impact of getting cancer at an earlier stage of life.”

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Inside the addictive architecture of the AI microdrama
articles.summary: Microdramas introduce an ingenious twist to the familiar psychology of the infinite scroll: monetize the cliffhanger.

items: Microdramas, or duanju, are short, addictive narratives designed to capture viewers' time and attention, monetizing cliffhangers through a combination of behavioral psychology and AI.

These platforms, like ReelShort and DramaBox, require users to make frequent economic decisions, leading to potential costs that can far exceed traditional streaming services like Netflix and Disney+.

The rise of microdramas poses a significant challenge to legacy streaming platforms, as audiences increasingly prefer quick, engaging content over longer formats, impacting their viewing habits and loyalty.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The 90-second melodramas flickering across our phone screens are no longer mere digital junk food.

Behind the frantic cliffhangers, the barrage of interstitial ads, and the constant badgering for virtual coins lies a multibillion-dollar enterprise engineered with behavioral psychology, algorithms, and artificial intelligence (AI). It has set its sights on the one asset legacy streaming giants cannot manufacture: our time.

The tropes are unmistakable to anyone who has idled through Facebook, TikTok, or YouTube. A billionaire masquerades as a pauper. A wife discovers her husband cheating with her sister. An abused daughter turns out to be the rightful heiress to an empire. Dragons, werewolves, competing for crowns, thrones and what not. A ruthless CEO falls hopelessly in love with an ordinary subordinate. The acting is often stilted, the plots unhinged, and the dialogue rarely resembles anything spoken by living humans.
Yet we do not look away.

An installment barely lasts two minutes before its successor cues itself. Just as the villain faces ruin or the heroine brandishes proof that she owns the company, the frame snaps to black. The resolution is held hostage: download the application to see what comes next. Only then does it become clear that what looked like silly social media distraction is actually the entrance to a ruthlessly calibrated money-making machine.
This is the domain of the vertical microdrama, or duanju, a narrative format that exploded in China before sweeping across the globe.

Where conventional TV requires 30 to 60 minutes to nurture a conflict and coax it to resolution, the microdrama strips narrative arc down to pure adrenaline, compressing tension and catharsis into 60 to 180 seconds. Betrayal, humiliation, revenge, and revelation arrive in rapid succession. Just before the brain registers satisfaction, the screen cuts out, dangling another hook.

A 2026 study of 658 participants established clear pathways linking narrative immersion, emotional involvement, algorithmic personalization, and compulsive viewing habits. Microdramas introduce an ingenious twist to the familiar psychology of the infinite scroll: they monetize the cliffhanger.
In this context, legacy streaming models seem almost quaint.

Netflix asks for payment once a month and surrenders its entire vault. A microdrama app demands an economic decision every few minutes. Watch an advertisement. Earn coins. Spend coins. Unlock 90 seconds of the next episode. Buy another bundle. Or capitulate to a recurring subscription.

On the Philippine App Store, ReelShort lists purchases and memberships at P299 and P499, including an auto-renewing P499 weekly subscription. DramaBox operates on a parallel tier of P299 and P499 memberships.

The arithmetic is startling. Sustained for four weeks, a P499 weekly tier totals P1,996. For perspective, Netflix Philippines charges P169 a month for Mobile, P279 for Basic, P449 for Standard, and P619 for Premium. Disney+ revised its Philippine monthly fees in December 2025 to P289 for Basic and P599 for Premium, while HBO Max remains leaner still at P149 for Mobile, P269 for Standard, and P399 for Ultimate.
A month of vertical melodrama can eclipse 11 months of Netflix Mobile, nearly seven months of Netflix Basic, seven months of Disney+ Basic, or over seven months of Max Standard.

blocks.caption: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study

blocks.text: To be sure, this is not an exact parallel: a ReelShort subscriber gains access to a broad library instead of paying P1,996 for a single series, and users can reduce or avoid out-of-pocket costs through rewarded tasks and ad sequences.
Yet that qualification merely underlines the brilliance of the trap. When viewers do not pay with money, they pay with time and attention.

The price of the cliffhanger. ReelShort’s Philippine App Store listing shows a P499 weekly subscription. Four consecutive weekly periods would therefore cost P1,996. The graph shows how far the same amount would go on conventional streaming services: roughly 13.4 months of Max Mobile, 11.8 months of Netflix Mobile, 7.4 months of Max Standard, 7.2 months of Netflix Basic, 6.9 months of Disney+ Basic, five months of Max Ultimate, 4.4 months of Netflix Standard, 3.3 months of Disney+ Premium or 3.2 months of Netflix Premium. The comparison does not mean watching a single microdrama necessarily costs P1,996—viewers can use ads, rewards and other payment options. Rather, it illustrates how quickly a seemingly modest P499 weekly auto-renewing charge can add up compared with the monthly subscription model of mainstream streaming platforms.

The “free” tier is an illusion of thrift. ReelShort itself notes that content can be unlocked through optional ads and rewarded tasks, while App Store reviews describe viewers dutifully sitting through commercial breaks to tease out the next narrative turn.
DramaBox users face the identical trade-off. The transaction is fluid — money, attention, or time — and the narrative is sculpted to ensure the user surrenders at least one value metric.

These micro-transactions swell into an immense commercial tide. Sensor Tower estimates short-drama apps generated roughly US$750 million in in-app revenue in the first quarter of 2026 alone, while downloads exceeded 850 million.

Omdia estimates the broader global microdrama industry could generate around US$14 billion this year. China already commands an audience of more than 800 million microdrama viewers, while AI is transforming what was already a high-speed production line into something that resembles an entertainment factory.

The role of AI is surgical. These productions are not purely synthetic; human actors, writers, directors, and crews still populate sets. But machine learning increasingly assists in drafting scripts, producing synthetic imagery and voices, automating localization and dubbing, generating visual effects, and testing plot variations across global markets. It enables a cadence of imitation, adaptation, and output that traditional Hollywood could never match.

Filipinos sit squarely in its path. DramaBox and ReelShort hold the No. 2 and No. 3 spots, respectively, in the Entertainment category of Apple’s Philippine App Store. Domestic powerhouses like ABS-CBN have entered vertical drama production, as Southeast Asia cements its status as one of the world’s most lucrative hubs for short-drama downloads.

The danger to Netflix, Disney+, and broadcast television is not an overnight wave of cancellations. It is a war of attrition over the clock. American mobile viewers already devote substantial daily hours to microdramas, while Southeast Asian audiences increasingly treat them as a surrogate for long-form video.

There are only so many hours between arriving home and going to sleep. Every forty minutes spent unraveling whether a mistreated but brilliant wife takes revenge on her cheating billionaire husband is 40 minutes permanently denied to prestige cinema, network broadcasts, or flagship series.

Legacy studios spent billions building sprawling libraries under the assumption that sheer abundance would guarantee audience loyalty. The architects of the microdrama discovered something far more potent: ordinary viewers do not always hunger for a two-hour movie. Frequently, our resolve dissolves before 90 seconds of unrestrained melodrama, an outrageous premise, and an unanswered question.
And the very moment our curiosity is piqued to discover what happens next, the price of finding out has already been calculated.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

This analysis draws from: Sensor Tower’s State of Short Drama Apps 2026; Omdia’s 2026 microdrama market and mobile-engagement research; Apple Philippines App Store listings for ReelShort and DramaBox; Netflix Philippines; Disney+ Philippine pricing; and Max Philippine pricing. The accompanying graph was generated by Vantage Point with raw data computed on Excel and exported to Photoshop for enhancement. The chart compares four P499 weekly ReelShort subscription periods (P1,996) with prevailing monthly rates of major streaming services.

articles.title: Alan Jones corresponded with 13-year-old who asked for financial help, court hears
articles.summary:
Radio host took teenager to lunch, had him visit his apartment, and told him to keep some conversations secret, court hears

  • Get our

blocks.text: Alan Jones corresponded extensively with a 13-year-old who had written to him asking for financial help, showering the teenager with praise and asking him to keep some secrets from his mother.

The teenager, known as complainant A, posted a letter to Jones after his father left, a family member died and his single mother was struggling financially, the court heard on the first day of evidence given by complainant A in a closed court.
The fifth and final complainant is one of five men who allege Jones sexually touched them between 2003 and 2020.

Jones, who has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching, replied that the young correspondent was a “sophisticated, articulate 13-year-old” who was experiencing “terrible circumstances”.

The 2GB broadcaster offered to help the family and over three years continued contact with the son over email, texts and phone calls. Jones also visited the family at home and on one occasion drove to the house but asked the teenager to come outside to meet him and did not go inside.
He took the teenager to lunch alone at a pub and had him visit him at his Circular Quay apartment twice.
He told the court the butler, David Allan, made him a hot breakfast on one occasion.
During their lengthy correspondence Jones asked for specific details of his mother’s financial distress with housing, employment and superannuation.
“I pioneered the expression ‘Struggle Street’ and I know that’s where you and your mother live,” Jones said in one of the hundreds of emails read out in the Downing Centre court on Tuesday.
Jones signed off his emails: “Lots of love and best wishes, Alan Jones AO,” adding phrases such as “You’re always in my thoughts” and “You are a wonderful young man”.
Jones asked the teenager on several occasions to keep certain details from his mother, suggesting that she was shouldering enough worry as it was.
On one occasion he disclosed to the then-16-year-old that he had just signed a cheque for $86,000 for building work to his mother’s home and added: “That’s just between you and me.”
Complainant A told the court he assured Jones that he was keeping certain conversations confidential, but in reality he would always tell his mother.
After offering to pay for a lawyer to assist the family, Jones wrote to say that the bill was $5,500 and there were limits to his generosity and he “can’t be an endless dripping tap”.
Jones wrote that “lawyers keep the meter running” and “I am not a mobile bank but I am here to help”.
When the teenager suggested he and his mother start paying him back, Jones responded: “I don’t expect any of it back.”

In opening statements, prosecutor Georgina Wright told the court that Jones invited the then 17-year-old complainant A to visit his farm in Fitzroy Falls in the New South Wales Southern Highlands where he allegedly kissed him on the mouth and touched him on the bottom.
The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

articles.title: Dizon explains P11.49-B DPWH budget increase for 2027
articles.summary: Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said the P11.49-billion increase in the proposed budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways for 2027 recommended by the Budget Amendments Review…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 11:38am

Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said the P11.49-billion increase in the proposed budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) for 2027 recommended by the Budget Amendments Review Sub-Committee (BARSC) of the House Committee on Appropriations would fund infrastructure projects that have recently completed the required documentation.

According to Dizon, some local road and flood mitigation projects were not included in the original P643.95-billion DPWH budget proposal because they had yet to comply with documentary and implementation requirements.

“Hindi lahat eh, lalong lalo na 'yung mga local roads. Kailangan natin 'yan eh kasi 'yung mga national roads naman mostly ‘yan maintenance na lang at kaunti na lang 'yan,” Dizon said during an inspection in Manila.
(Not all [were included in the proposed budget], especially the [construction of] local roads. We need those because the national roads would just need maintenance and there are just a few of them.)

Dizon stressed that all projects must undergo strict screening and comply with the agency’s requirements before they can be funded and implemented. He said these projects later completed the requirements, prompting the request for additional funding. He also assured the public that the DPWH would closely monitor the use of the funds to help prevent corruption.

“Walang proyekto na hindi puwedeng walang kumpletong requirements: program of works, plano, kasama dapat sa master plan ng mga LGUs and kasama din sa master plan ng mga river basins natin lalo na kung iyan ay flood mitigation. Kailangan ‘yan may no objection sa mga LGU kasi ayaw na natin maulit 'yung hindi coordinated ang mga proyekto sa mga LGU,” Dizon added.

(No project will be allowed to have incomplete requirements. The program of works, plan should be included in the master plan of LGUs and in the master plan of our river basins, especially if that is for flood mitigation. The LGU should have no objection to the project because we want to avoid having projects that are not coordinated with LGUs.)

The BARSC on October 1 recommended an additional P11.49 billion for the DPWH, with more than half earmarked for national road projects. The proposed increase still requires approval from the full House Committee on Appropriations and the House plenary.

ACT Teachers Representative and Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio called for a full disclosure of project lists, proponents, allocation criteria, and funding sources after the BARSC approved P77.86 billion in "pork-type amendments" for the 2027 proposed national budget.
The P77.86-B "pork-type" amendments account for 67% of the P116.32-B total amendments approved by BARSC on October 1 and 2, Tinio said.

The "pork-type" amendments are for the following programs: DPWH capital outlay, Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), farm-to-market roads, Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), Medical Assistance for Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP), TUPAD, and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS).

“These amendments show that pork has not disappeared from the national budget. It has merely been repackaged under institutional amendments, local government support, infrastructure lump sums, and cash assistance programs. Pinalaki ang infrastructure pork at ayuda," Tinio said.
(The infrastructure pork and cash aid were given more allocations.)

“Meanwhile, no additional funds were provided for PERA (Personnel Economic Relief Allowance), despite the clamor to raise the current proposal of an additional Php 500 per month for government employees on top of the current Php 2000 to a more substantial amount. They have been waiting 17 years for a PERA increase. Neither were amendments provided for teacher pay or additional plantilla positions. DepEd’s Php 6.61-billion request for ARAL and learning recovery was not acted upon, while ARAL received only Php 350 million. These figures expose the distorted priorities of the amendments,” the lawmaker said.
Tinio also said amendments for DPWH roads and convergence projects were presented without named projects or locations.
He also said that P11.49 billion in DPWH institutional amendments were not itemized. —RSD/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecutor: 6-hour questioning of AMLC witness due to Defense's objections
articles.summary: The direct examination of Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura took six hours on Monday due to numerous objections by the defense, House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 11:28am

The direct examination of Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura took six hours on Monday due to numerous objections by the defense, House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro Party-list said on Tuesday.

Ridon was responding to defense counsel Sheila Sison’s manifestation before the Senate impeachment court that they should not be rushed in conducting their cross examination on Monday, October 5. The defense panel was eventually allowed by the impeachment court to continue today its cross examination on Tuesday.

“It won’t last for six hours if the defense is not objecting every hour. Most of the time, the defense has been objecting that entire time. It wasn't because we had so many questions. It was really because they kept on objecting on each question. That needs to be stated for the record,” he said ahead of the Day 34 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President.
“It is their right, but we have to say that the long hours was not just because we kept asking for questions,” he added.
Ridon said if the truth takes time, then the prosecution is all for it.

“The most important thing here is for the truth to come out. How long does it take for the truth to come up, for the nation to know what had happened on the finance of transactions of the vice president, the husband, and their firms, then we will take that long,” he said.

“But think of the figures as staggering: P4.4 billion in covered and suspicious transactions of the Duterte couple and P5 billion on Duterte-related firms. How can they have that much money,” Ridon added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Remulla flags Customs' alleged 'lack of data sharing' in smuggling cases
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has raised concerns about the Bureau of Customs' supposed lack of cooperation and data sharing, warning that missing or delayed documentation is hindering efforts to…

blocks.text: October 6, 2026 | 11:19am

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla responds to senators’ questions regarding the Philippines’ residual obligations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) following its withdrawal from the tribunal, during a public hearing on Thursday, April 10, 2025.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has raised concerns about the Bureau of Customs' (BOC) supposed lack of cooperation and data sharing, warning that missing or delayed documentation is hindering efforts to prosecute smuggling cases and strengthen anti-smuggling initiatives.

In a DZRH radio interview, Remulla said that while other government agencies have opened their records for joint anti-corruption and law enforcement efforts, the BOC remains hesitant to provide complete case documentation.
“Nagkaroon kami ng meeting ng Customs at saka ng DOJ (Department of Justice) para nga tumigil na ang kalokohang ito sa smuggling,” Remulla said.
(We had a meeting with Customs and the DOJ precisely to put an end to this nonsense in smuggling.)
“Ang problema nga kasi 'yung sa Customs, ayaw nila kumpletuhin ang documentation para ma-dismiss ang kaso,” he added.
(The problem with Customs is that they refuse to complete the documentation, causing the case to be dismissed.)
Remulla explained that while his office initiates cases or conducts investigations, their requests for necessary records are repeatedly met with inaction due to a lack of data sharing.

He noted that unlike the Bureau of Customs, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has already agreed to a data-sharing arrangement, adding that his office will now challenge Customs to do the same.
“Ifa-file namin ang kaso o kaya iimbestigahan namin sabay kapag hinihingi namin ang dokumento ayaw dumating ang dokumento. Walang data sharing,” Remulla said.
(We will file the case or conduct an investigation, but when we request the necessary documents, they refuse to provide them. There is no data sharing.)

Remulla voiced these concerns amid the government's heightened anti-smuggling drive, which has recently led to several contraband seizures by the BOC, as well as joint inter-agency operations with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and other law enforcement bodies.
The DOJ, the NBI and the BOC previously entered into a memorandum of agreement designed to curb economic sabotage. Remulla witnessed the signing.

articles.title: Sara Duterte lawyer apologizes to senator-judges over remarks on confidentiality rules
articles.summary: Defense counsel Mark Vinluan apologized Tuesday to senator-judges over his remarks during the cross examination of Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC),…

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 11:18am

Defense counsel Mark Vinluan apologized Tuesday to senator-judges over his remarks during the cross examination of Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), wherein the former repeatedly pointed out that disclosure of bank transactions could mean jail time for all those who will use the information.
"We just want to test the credibility of the witness," Vinluan said during Day 34 of the impeachment court of Vice President Sara Duterte.
"It is never our intention to cause intimidation to the members of the Honorable impeachment court. I personally apologize and I can commit to be more circumspect moving forward," Vinluan added.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero noted Vinluan's manifestation, saying it was "well-taken."

On Monday, Vinluan repeatedly underscored that Section 8A of the Anti-Money Laundering Act which provides that the Anti-Money Laundering Council or AMLC and its secretariat should securely protect information, received or processed and shall not reveal in any manner any information known to them by reason of their office.

As such, Vinulan said, "the law prohibits the disclosure in any manner of confidential information including those submitted by the banks and other covered persons to the AMLC" and that this prohibition "extends to the members of the media which are here today for the purpose of broadcasting these proceedings to the general public."

"The defense, therefore, respectfully submits that allowing this witness to testify will breach confidentiality, violate the law, and disregard the explicit warning by the AMLC, all in violation of the respondent accused rights. We, therefore, put on record that defense is not and will not be complicit in breaking the law," Vinluan said.
Senator-judge Vicente Sotto III responded by saying that the defense should be reminded that the members of Congress have parliamentary immunity in exercising their mandate.

Senator-judges Raffy Tulfo and Francis Pangilinan shared Sotto’s sentiments, saying that the defense should not go around making threats, and that the defense should go to the Supreme Court if they feel that they are aggrieved with the disclosure of AMLC records.
For her part, senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said journalists should not be threatened from reporting the goings on in the impeachment trial of the vice president. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Is a second, stickier inflation wave taking shape?
articles.summary: There is also the elephant in the room: the looming 'super' El Niño.

blocks.text: There is also the elephant in the room: the looming 'super' El Niño.

items: Inflation in the Philippines rose to 7.2% in September, with significant increases across various commodity groups, particularly in food, energy, and housing rents.
National Statistician Dennis Mapa highlighted that the inflation trend is broad and persistent, with 11 out of 13 major commodity groups experiencing faster inflation compared to August.
Risks remain high due to factors like the recent fare increases in public transport and the potential impact of a looming 'super' El Niño on food supply.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Even after stripping out seasonal effects, inflation is steadily marching up, with price increases now spreading across most commodity groups and regions and several risks still not captured by the latest data.

Asked by Rappler whether the surge in September inflation could mark the beginning of a second, stickier inflation wave, National Statistician Dennis Mapa pointed to the seasonally adjusted figures, which showed month-on-month inflation accelerating to 1.1% in September from 0.5% in August.
“Even on the seasonally adjusted time series, the trajectory is still going up,” Mapa said in a mix of English and Filipino on Tuesday, October 6.
While some of September’s increase could fade as weather-related disruptions ease, Mapa said other sources of inflation could prove harder to unwind.
“There are items that we’re seeing now that are, as you mentioned, somewhat sticky,” he said, pointing particularly to energy, transport, and housing rents.
Headline inflation jumped to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, returning to the level last seen in April. The last time inflation was higher was in March 2023, when it reached 7.6%.
Average inflation from January to September stood at 5.4% , remaining well above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%.

Mapa also noted that the uptick in inflation was unusually broad. Eleven of the 13 major commodity groups posted faster inflation than in August, while 16 of the country’s 18 regions saw inflation pick up. Mapa described such a widespread monthly increase across commodity groups as “quite rare.”
“We are seeing quite a lot of risks,” he said in Filipino.

Food remained the biggest source of pressure. Food and non-alcoholic beverages posted 6.7% inflation and accounted for 73.4% of the increase in headline inflation from August. Vegetable prices swung back up after declining the previous month, while rice, fish, and other food items also became more expensive. Rice inflation alone reached 20.3%.
Some of that pressure could still prove temporary. Mapa said vegetable prices often rise after typhoons and flooding before easing once production and supply normalize.

But other components appear harder to unwind. Mapa pointed to energy, transport, and housing rents as among the items showing more persistent pressure. In September, electricity inflation reached 14.6%, gasoline 40.9%, diesel 61.3%, while rents rose 4%. Rental costs have a strong weight on inflation, and Mapa noted that increases here could affect the overall inflation rate.

Core inflation, which excludes selected volatile food and energy items, also accelerated to 4.7% from 4.1% in August, its highest level since October 2023. Mapa said 10 of the 13 commodity groups used in the core measure posted month-on-month increases, another sign that price pressures were not just confined to food and fuel.
And unfortunately, more pressure may still be coming.

The September figures did not yet fully capture the recent increases in jeepney, bus, and taxi fares, which took effect only in the final days of the month. These are expected to show up more clearly in October.
There is also the elephant in the room: the looming “super” El Niño, which Mapa said will elevate risks to food supply.

“We hope that it will go down,” he said, but added that the breadth of September’s increase showed “there are a lot of risks,” particularly among heavily weighted items such as food, energy, and transport. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 5: Longest trial day as AMLC bares records
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court held its longest hearing yet on Monday, October 5, where the Anti-Money Laundering Council's chief testified to P4.4 billion in reported transactions involving Vice…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court held its longest hearing yet on Monday, October 5, where the Anti-Money Laundering Council's chief testified to P4.4 billion in reported transactions involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, including P319 million in remittances from China to his food company.

AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified as a prosecution witness under Article II of the impeachment complaint. That article accuses Duterte of amassing wealth "manifestly disproportionate to her lawful income," and of failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband's assets in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) for 2022, 2023 and 2024.
His testimony took up the entire eight-hour session and drew repeated objections from the defense and sharp exchanges among senator-judges over whether the records should be disclosed at all.
The AMLC presentation had been moved from October 1 at the defense's request, after prosecutors also dropped former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV from their witness list.
Monday's hearing came as House prosecutors have confirmed they would no longer present Article III, the bribery charge.
Here are the four highlights from the proceedings on Monday, October 5.
1. Court allows AMLC records, including dollar accounts, over objections

Before Buenaventura could testify, defense counsel Mark Vinluan moved to exclude him on the basis of the confidentiality provision in the Anti-Money Laundering Act, which bars the AMLC from revealing information in any manner.
The defense had attempted to convince the court that the AMLA provisions do not single out impeachment as an exception to its "absolute" prohibition for sharing AMLC records.
Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero denied the motion and sided with the prosecution in ruling that confidentiality provisions do not make AMLC reports "absolutely immune from compulsory process."
The impeachment court ruled that Section 8A "regulates the manner and conditions of disclosure" but "does not command absolute silence under every circumstance."

Escudero cited the Supreme Court's ruling in Republic v. Sandiganbayan and the Bank Secrecy Law's express exception for impeachment cases, which he said confirms "that bank secrecy is not an absolute bar to the constitutional accountability process."

He limited Buenaventura's testimony to the subpoenaed reports and said parts could be heard behind closed doors if needed. "This ruling does not authorize unrestricted public disclosure," Escudero said.

The ruling divided the senator-judges. Sen. Pia Cayetano noted that the anti-money laundering law, unlike the bank secrecy law, contains no exception for impeachment. She said reading one into it "puts a cloud over the impeachment proceedings." Sen. Imee Marcos similarly argued there was "no mention of an exception for impeachment proceedings."

Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, one of the law's two primary sponsors in 2001, said lawmakers intended the confidentiality rule to bind banks and not the AMLC. He said it "would be absurd that a private bank in an impeachment case trial can be compelled to divulge bank records" while the AMLC could not.

The dispute resurfaced in the afternoon, when Buenaventura, on direct examination, was made to testify on the figures of a foreign currency account. Marcos objected, saying it was "well established in both the Erap and Corona impeachments that foreign currency accounts are excluded."

Escudero overruled her with a prepared ruling that said the confidentiality provisions of the Foreign Currency Deposit Act must be read in tandem with the Anti-Money Laundering Act. Since banks are required to report covered and suspicious transactions to the AMLC regardless of currency, that means such information cannot be concealed by the council from the impeachment court.

The presiding officer also cited the 2012 impeachment trial of former Supreme Court Chief Justice Renato Corona, where then Ombudsman Conchita Carpio-Morales was allowed to testify on an AMLC report on the chief justice's foreign currency accounts.
2. What the AMLC records showed
Divinagracia said the records were meant to establish a baseline of Duterte's wealth and a "pattern of non-disclosure."
According to the AMLC summary, covered and suspicious transaction reports involving Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, totaled P4.4 million from 2007 to 2025.

Buenaventura said about P1.63 billion of this was money coming into the accounts and P1.31 billion was money going out. The remaining P1.46 billion consisted of "fund transactions that could not be reliably classified as inflows or outflows due to insufficient, incomplete, or ambiguous sender and or beneficiary information," most of them from before 2014.

He said the total was lower than the roughly P6.7 billion the AMLC reported earlier because the court's subpoena covered a different period and all reporting institutions, not just banks, and because one bank, the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), corrected its reports.
Escudero had the AMLC chief confirm that the figures cover only covered and suspicious transactions and would not mirror the full bank records.

Buenaventura testified that seven inter-account transfers totalling P193.71 million, all in a single day on March 28, 2014, involved a BPI joint account of former President Rodrigo Duterte and the vice president.

He also identified a P20-million cash purchase of a life insurance policy on April 1, 2014, a debit of nearly P9.8 million from the same joint account in 2011, and a withdrawal of more than P9 million in 2013.
Buenaventura also confirmed that more recent records showed large cash movements in her or her husband's bank accounts during her term as vice president.

Six transactions all in a single day on Aug. 6, 2024, specifically two check encashments and four over-the-counter withdrawals of between P3 million and P15 million each, took P41 million out of her husband Manases Carpio's account in a single day.

Reports in the vice president's records showed a P2.37-million withdrawal at Landbank on Dec. 5, 2024. On Dec. 20, 2024, a P5.97-million withdrawal at BDO and a P1.7-million check encashment at Metrobank followed, 11 days before December 31, the cutoff date for assets declared in officials' SALNs.
Buenaventura also testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., the banana chips exporter company of Duterte's husband, received P319.33 million in remittances from mainland China and Hong Kong.
Broken down, the AMLC chief confirmed that of the 143 covered transaction reports on those remittances, 141 involved China and two involved Hong Kong.
The amount is close to the figure Trillanes presented at a press conference last week after withdrawing as a witness.
The records named Jinhua Dongxi Trading Co., Ltd. and China National Township among the counterparties.
Cale88 was among the companies Duterte declared she was a stockholder of in her SALN.
An AMLC information-sharing report also listed the vice president as the beneficiary of checks worth P14.88 million bought in 2011 and 2012 by Samuel Cang Uy and two others.
3. Suspicious transaction reports show Duterte's transactions were flagged by banks
The trial took a more surprising turn when the prosecution drew out Buenaventura's testimony on the suspicious transaction reports filed on the vice president.

Several of these reports on Duterte that were read in court were filed by banks and insurers on the basis of news reports, action that Buenaventura said is within the ambit of these institutions given the "threshold is suspicion" but which some senator-judges called unreliable.

Under the anti-money laundering law, banks and other institutions must file a covered transaction report for any cash transaction above P500,000 in a single banking day. A suspicious transaction report is filed when the institution sees red flags, regardless of the amount.
Buenaventura said the AMLC holds 34 suspicious transaction reports on Duterte from 2007 to 2025, while at least 30 such reports involved her husband, bringing the total to 55 for the couple.
The prosecutor had Buenaventura read some of the suspicious transaction reports.

For instance, two 2019 transactions by Duterte involving insurance premium payments to Mercantile Insurance Company Inc. were flagged for "graft and corrupt practices" after "several news outlets recently released a list of individuals and corporations identified as being involved in the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) flood control issue."
Buenaventura also read a suspicious transaction report filed by BDO Life Assurance on a Dec. 5, 2024 transaction, which cites "malversation of public funds and property."
Reading the narrative, the AMLC chief says: "The client is alleged to have misappropriated confidential funds to her office in the Office of the Vice President (OVP)."
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano faulted the AMLC for passing on the reports and equated them to reading out "baseless rumors" in open court.

However, Sen. Kiko Pangilinan said he preferred to give banks the "benefit of the doubtm" while Sen. Risa Hontiveros said she would wait for testimony from the banks and the BIR before dismissing the banks' reports as rumors.

Pia Cayetano objected to the prosecution's on-screen summaries of the reports, saying they "do not show an accurate picture of what the witness is testifying to." She said: "This is like reading volume two of a comics and I never even saw volume one of the comic book."
4. Defense questions AMLC chief's authority; senator-judges push back

In cross-examination, Vinluan established that Buenaventura heads only the AMLC secretariat. He is not a member of the council itself, which consists of the Bangko Sentral governor, the insurance commissioner and the Securities and Exchange Commission chairman, and which must act unanimously.
Buenaventura confirmed he was appointed on April 14, 2026, eight days before he disclosed the couple's records to the House justice committee on April 22.

Asked whether the three council members gave him written authority for that disclosure and for his testimony on Monday, Buenaventura said he relied on information-sharing guidelines the council approved in 2022 and that he informed the council by memo. He said the House did not ask for such authority.

When Vinluan cited the administrative and criminal penalties under the anti-money laundering law, Divinagracia objected that he was bordering on badgering the witness. Sen. Raffy Tulfo then accused the defense of repeatedly trying to draw out redundant answers from Buenaventura and intimidating him.

Pangilinan said it was uncalled for to raise possible criminal liability over disclosures the court had already authorized. He also called out the defense for seemingly attempting to intimidate the impeachment court itself.
The defense will continue its cross-examination of Buenaventura on Tuesday, October 6.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte's camp: AMLC exec's testimony doesn't prove money illegally sourced
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday shrugged off claims that the testimony of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura during the impeachment trial…

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published October 6, 2026 11:03am

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday shrugged off claims that the testimony of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura during the impeachment trial supposedly confirmed the allegations made by former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV, saying that the witness did not prove that the funds were illegally sourced.
In a statement, Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., Duterte’s spokesperson, said that Buenaventura only testified on covered and suspicious transactions reports filed by banks.
“If anything was confirmed, it is only that Trillanes obtained his information illegally in violation of the Anti-Money Laundering Act and Bank Secrecy Laws,” Panelo said.

“[Buenaventura] did not, because he could not, confirm, and the prosecution still has to prove, that any money attributed to the Vice President was illegally sourced, was hidden, or was even hers to begin with,” he added.
To recall, Trillanes accused the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio, of respectively accepting P150 million and P319 million through their separate organizations.
He also alleged that Duterte failed to declare in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth her peso and dollar time deposit and insurance.
During the impeachment trial on Monday, Buenaventura testified that the AMLC recorded P4.4 billion in covered and suspicious bank transactions under the names of Duterte and Carpio.
The AMLC official also confirmed that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Carpio, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
Duterte’s spokesman slammed Trillanes’ claims, calling the former senator a “professional anti-Duterte propagandist.”

“Trillanes is no truth-teller. He is a professional anti-Duterte propagandist who tried to fill the gaps in the prosecution’s evidence with hearsay, rumors, malicious speculation, and outright lies, delivered at a press conference where none of it could be scrutinized,” Panelo said.
“Senator-Judge Lacson himself has confirmed that his accusations have no probative value. His allegations are better suited for the parlor, not the court,” he added.
GMA News Online reached out to Trillanes regarding the matter, but said he has “no comment” as of posting time. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Youth groups ask SC to block law postponing barangay, SK polls to 2028
articles.summary: This is the second petition that was filed assailing the said law, which postponed the BSKE elections that were supposed to be scheduled on November 2.

blocks.text: October 6, 2026 | 11:03am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
MANILA, Philippines — Youth groups challenged before the Supreme Court on Monday, October 5, the law that postponed the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
This is the second petition filed assailing the said law, which postponed the BSKE elections that were supposed to be held on November 2.

The petitioners are seeking a Petition for Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus, along with an extremely urgent prayer for a Temporary Restraining Order and/or Writ of Preliminary Mandatory Injunction to halt the law's implementation.

In their petition, the youth leaders strongly criticized the 20th Congress for repeatedly altering election schedules and terms. They pointed out that the legislature recently lengthened the term of barangay officials from three years to four years, and has now pushed it further to five years under the law.

“A very recent postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) through a ‘term-setting law’ was already ONE TOO MANY. ANOTHER, SUCCESSIVE resetting exposes the danger of allowing legislative form to prevail over constitutional limitations. It is a CIRCUMVENTION, IN BROAD DAYLIGHT, of the very five-point guidelines laid down by this Honorable Court in Macalintal,” the group’s petition read.
The respondents named in the petition are the Office of the President, Commission on Elections, House of Representatives, and the Senate of the Philippines.
The first petition was filed by election law expert Romulo Macalintal on September 28.
Macalintal argued that the law infringes on the electorate's right of suffrage under the guise of "fixing" the term of barangay officials at five years.
The last BSKE was held on Oct. 30, 2023, while the next elections were originally scheduled for December 2025.
Congress later moved the polls to November 2026 through Republic Act 12232, which also adjusted the term of office to four years.
Republic Act 12326, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on September 24, meanwhile, postpones the elections by another two years to November 2028.

The U.S. Coast Guard has named all six people, including four Canadians, aboard an Ontario-based air ambulance that went missing off the coast of Massachusetts on Saturday.
Safety Board of Canada will be leading the investigation into the incident
The U.S. Coast Guard has named all six people, including four Canadians, who were aboard an Ontario-based air ambulance that went missing off the coast of Massachusetts on Saturday.
The Canadians are Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. The two Bermudians are Marilyn Lavonne Bean and Sergio Wayne Lottimore.

"During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, Commander of the U.S. Coast Guard Northeast District, said in a statement.
"We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation."
The statement added that the Safety Board of Canada will be leading the investigation into the incident.

articles.title: Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
articles.summary: The Parti Québécois, which secured a minority, has vowed to hold an independence referendum in the years to come.

blocks.text: Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.

It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.
The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month.
The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.
Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.

Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030.
Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.
He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.
He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead.
"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.

For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness.
Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.
His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.
Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.
Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government.
The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.

Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters.
Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.
Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition.
"Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart."
The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.

Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.
Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province.
Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party.

"Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

articles.title: Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
articles.summary: Schmidt acknowledged that his actions "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt".

blocks.text: Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.

In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.

Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.

It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

articles.title: Trump says taxpayers will no longer fund ads touting administration
articles.summary: Trump faced criticism from across the political divide after at least $1.5 million in federal funds was spent on TV ads. He says his MAGA Inc. super PAC will pay for future ads.

image.caption: According to The New York Times, Trump ⁠personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots [FILE: Sept 30, 2026]Image: Bonnie Cash/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said Monday that taxpayer funds will no longer be used for television ads featuring him, which he claimed were a "standard thing to do," and said the cost will instead be borne by his super PAC.
The campaign-style ads, which cost at least $1.5 million (€1.34 million) in federal funds, drew criticism from lawmakers and ethics experts across the political divide.
What did Trump say about the ads?
Labeling the ads a "positive promotion for our Great USA," the US president said he decided to bear the costs himself and through his MAGA Inc. political action committee.

"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
A White House official confirmed that MAGA Inc. would fund the ads going forward.
The MAGA Inc. super PAC had a war chest of more than $400 million by the end of July.
Trump ads warn of 'final battle'
The ads, which began airing in late September, feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."
They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.
Critics, including lawmakers from both parties, have questioned whether the ads violate restrictions on government propaganda and partisan political activity.
Democrats have said the administration transferred $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to fund the ads and have called for independent investigations.
Trump has not said whether taxpayers will be reimbursed for the ads already aired.

articles.title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad, in first since World War Two
articles.summary: The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan will be the first military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since the end of World War Two.

blocks.text: The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Malik Hasan, a US Army major and physician, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder by a jury panel of 13 officers, which unanimously recommended his death sentence.
Parnell said the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.

The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.

Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.

The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title: MovePH welcomes new Movers for community action, local storytelling
articles.summary: More than 30 youth leaders, campus journalists, and advocates join Rappler’s civic engagement arm as it expands the Movers Program from community storytelling to civic action

items: Rappler's MovePH program welcomed a new cohort of local volunteers, known as Movers, to enhance community engagement and social advocacy.
The program emphasizes collaboration between journalists and community members to amplify local stories and address social issues, as highlighted by Rappler executives.
The expanded Movers program allows for greater participation and skill development among volunteers, enabling them to lead initiatives that reflect their communities' needs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – To grow its network of changemakers and local community volunteers, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH welcomed a new cohort of Movers to the program on Friday, October 2.
The expanded program seeks to equip local citizens not only to tell stories from their communities, but also to organize, collaborate, and mobilize their communities for social good.

The new cohort was onboarded during MovePH’s first nationwide orientation for its volunteers dubbed, “Community in Action: An Orientation to the Movers Program.” The virtual event brought together more than 30 youth leaders, campus journalists, and advocates from communities across the country.
In her welcoming remarks, Rappler executive editor Glenda Gloria highlighted the crucial role of Movers.

She recalled how back in the glorious days of social media, volunteers online helped amplify the campaign for the freedom of Mary Jane Veloso by initiating an online petition and coordinating with organizations that had long been working on her case.
At the time, those volunteers were not yet called Movers, Gloria said. “That’s when we decided on MovePH becoming the citizen arm of Rappler,” she added.
Gloria said the experience showed that journalists and communities have different but complementary roles in advancing issues and advocacies.
By working together, volunteers can bring their networks and local knowledge, while journalists can help document and amplify stories.
“We journalists alone cannot do it. Communities and volunteers alone cannot do it. It takes a village not just to survive, but also to change the future,” Gloria said.
This was also echoed by Pia Ranada, Rappler’s head of community. In her message to the Movers, she highlighted the knowledge and experiences that communities bring to civic work.
“What is the superpower of communities? Lived stories,” Ranada said.

She cited her work on public transportation accessibility as one example. Together with partner organizations and communities, they were able to examine the accessibility of Metro Manila’s train system for persons with disabilities.
The groups helped identify gaps and develop an audit of features to make public transportation systems accessible to PWDs.
For Ranada, involving communities from the start helped ensure that the work reflected the experiences of people who actually use the system.

The same approach has been used in Rappler’s Corruption Watch initiative, where Movers and other volunteers helped verify information on infrastructure projects in their communities. Volunteers checked projects and information from their own localities, helping the newsroom track details that may otherwise be difficult to verify remotely.
“Communities are force multipliers, and journalists are force multipliers of communities,” Ranada said. “We were able to create an impact that perhaps alone we could not have done.”
Ranada said the partnership also allows journalists to bring community experiences to a wider audience through reporting.
“When you put the storyteller and the stories together…stories powerfully told can move mountains and make change happen,” she added.

Jene-Anne Pangue, head of MovePH, explained that the Movers Program is a volunteer-based leadership program that provides participants with skills, networks, and opportunities to work on issues in their communities.

Pangue became a Mover in 2014 after experiencing Supertyphoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in Tacloban City. “As a Mover back in 2014, I helped amplify the stories of my local community in Tacloban post-Haiyan together with my campus publication,” she said.

Drawing from her experience as a Mover and now as part of the MovePH team, Pangue said the expanded program is designed to sustain its local volunteer network while creating space for both storytellers and civic leaders.
“What really ties the community storytellers and civic leaders are actually the stories that we want to tell,” Pangue said.
The Movers Program also provides more avenues for Movers to hone their skills and build meaningful connections with others in the network.
“We don’t discount the fact that you are experts in your fields,” Pangue told Movers.
Since 2012, MovePH has conducted more than 30 roadshows across the country, where communities and volunteers have participated in trainings and discussions on local issues and civic engagement.

The roadshows have been one way of training and recruiting Movers. Under the expanded program, volunteers can now apply to become Movers even without a roadshow being held in their area, while MovePH can continue organizing roadshows in different communities.

In recent years, Movers have supported coverage of local and national elections, anti-corruption efforts, Palarong Pambansa, and other major events in different parts of the country. Beyond event coverage, they have also highlighted inspiring actions, community initiatives, and advocacy efforts making a difference in their localities.
One of the new Movers is 21-year-old Shakira Mae Salas, an education student currently based in Aklan.
She plans to work on education access in upland communities through an initiative called “BundokAsyon” or Education for Students in Upland Areas.
She recalled traveling two to three hours from the town center and seeing classrooms with limited resources and teachers handling multiple grade levels in the same room.

“I want to achieve this initiative not just for those students in the upland areas to receive the education they want or they deserve, but also as a wake-up call for the local government of the struggle that the students and teachers have to endure every day,” she said.
Over the next few months, the new cohort will work with MovePH to highlight more local voices and stories, while supporting or leading community-led action.
Interested in becoming a Mover? Apply now. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bestselling author Steven Galloway's wife testifies on Day 1 of defamation trial
articles.summary: Former UBC professor and bestselling author Steven Galloway claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault made by multiple people over a decade ago.

image.caption: Steven Galloway is pictured in 2014 at his former office at the University of British Columbia. The first day of court proceedings in a defamation lawsuit filed by Galloway, a bestselling author, began on Monday. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Former UBC professor and bestselling author Steven Galloway claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault made by multiple people over a decade ago.
Former UBC writing professor claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault

The wife of former University of British Columbia (UBC) professor Steven Galloway was the first witness to testify on day one of the defamation trial against four defendants he says falsely accused him of sexual assault.
Galloway’s accuser is a former student, "AB", who is the main defendant in the lawsuit. Others named as defendants are alleged to have spread the sexual assault claim, including on social media.
Katie Wagner told the court that Galloway was at a speaking engagement in Ohio in late 2015 when he first became aware of the accusation.
Wagner says that, when she arrived in Ohio to support him, Galloway was in a hospital on 72-hour suicide watch.

"He was in a hospital gown, he was upset, crying, shaking. He knew there was an accusation of sexual assault, but of course, he hadn’t sexually assaulted anyone — so there was a lot of us trying to figure out what was going on," she told the court.

items: Defendant apologizes to B.C. writer days before defamation trial to start

blocks.text: Galloway, a bestselling Canadian author, was never criminally charged — though he was fired from his job as a tenured professor and chair of the UBC creative writing department.
A report by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd, commissioned by UBC, concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.
After arbitration, he was awarded over $240,000 in damages from the university.
'Never going to be an end'
Wagner said Boyd’s report only served to sparked a "mob of people online" to repeat the accusations.
"There would be a flurry on Twitter — which was such a big thing," said Wagner. "I think there was a sense at that point … that there was never going to be an end to it."
Wagner testified that the accusations and resulting firestorm has been hard on their four children, finances, and life in general.

She said Galloway became extremely withdrawn, and at one point she found him trying to hang himself with a rope. She also recounted strictly controlling his medications for fear he would intentionally overdose.

items: Canadian authors criticize UBC's handling of Steven Galloway case

blocks.text: Galloway sued numerous people for defamation in 2018. His accusers fought the case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.
The high court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants' arguments held, "there would be no legal consequences of any kind" to publicly calling someone a rapist.
At least nine of the defendants have settled out of court or issued apologies, including author Chelsea Rooney, whose lengthy statement of apology was published this past weekend.

Galloway is the author of novels including The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist. His lawyer said he is seeking special damages, to account for Galloway's former standing as a star in the literary world who had his career cut short.
AB has asked the court to keep her identity confidential over concerns an "online mob" would be unleashed against her.

Her counsel told the court that AB has attempted suicide. He said while news stories published about the case haven’t revealed her identity, people have named her in the comment sections under the articles.
The trial was originally scheduled for 60 days, but with fewer defendants, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma said it will likely take 20 days.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

items: Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.
