articles.title: High-flying lawyer goes on trial for writing bad cheque allegedly to cover for collapsing firm
articles.summary: A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed in a spectacular flameout three years ago, when millions of dollars of client money was discovered missing from the firm's…

image.caption: Suspended lawyer Nicholas Julian Cartel, accused of fraud for writing a bad cheque to allegedly cover a shortfall in his law firm's trust account, leaves a downtown Toronto courthouse on Monday during a break in his criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·CBC Investigates

A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed in a spectacular flameout three years ago, when millions of dollars of client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, is on trial on a charge of fraud stemming from the police investigation into the case.
Nicholas Cartel is self-representing against criminal charge stemming from probe into $7M embezzlement

A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed spectacularly three years ago, after millions of dollars in client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, went on trial Monday on a fraud charge stemming from the police investigation into the case.

Nicholas Cartel, 62, faces one count of fraud over $5,000 based on allegations that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque for $300,000 in an attempt to cover up a shortfall in the trust account at Cartel & Bui LLP, the firm he ran with his wife.

The alleged fraud occurred in February 2023, when Cartel & Bui LLP was handling a property sale for a client. The law firm needed to pay out $2.22 million in proceeds to the client but didn't have sufficient funds in its trust account because Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
Bui is facing 32 criminal charges in a separate case stemming from the embezzlement.

The February 2023 incident foreshadowed a series of events in which more than 25 property owners and buyers in southern Ontario ran into problems closing on real estate deals because money was missing from the Cartel & Bui trust account.
One couple lost $2.16 million they had entrusted to the firm to buy a house in Toronto, while other clients — or home-purchase insurers — were out as much as $729,000.

Cartel is not facing criminal charges in relation to those other cases, and has long maintained his innocence. He says he operated a separate legal practice at the firm focused on class actions and litigation, while the theft of client money occurred in the real estate side of the business run by his wife, Singa Bui.
With respect to the criminal charge alleging that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque, Cartel does not deny writing it but says his actions didn't amount to fraud.

He also maintains that prosecutors have improperly withheld evidence from him and misleadingly presented other evidence. At the outset of his trial Monday, he told the court he intends to bring an application under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to have his criminal charge stayed.
Bank employees testify

At the start of Monday's trial in provincial court in Toronto, prosecutor Dihim Emami called a witness from Royal Bank of Canada's investigations department to testify about records associated with the personal chequing account on which the $300,000 cheque was drawn.

The witness, Adkin Holder, a former Toronto police fraud-squad detective, testified that the account's opening documents showed it belonged to Cartel and that for months before the bad cheque was written, the account had a negative balance.

He said that because of that, a $300,000 cheque would have failed to cash, and the receiving bank could have been at risk of losing the money if it was unable to recover it from the person who wrote the cheque.
Cartel later asked Holder whether it was possible the account was in fact a joint account at the time the bad cheque was written, which Holder agreed was possible.
Prosecutors then entered records showing that the account statements bore only Cartel's name, while statements for other joint accounts bore both his name and Bui's.
A second witness, from TD Bank, where the law firm had its trust account, began testifying Monday afternoon about transactions in that account and is expected to resume Tuesday.
Already jailed for contempt of court

Cartel has already spent 30 days in jail over the collapse of his firm, after a judge in separate civil lawsuits against him and his wife ruled in August 2024 that he had committed contempt of court by failing to produce records or answer questions about where the missing trust-account money went.
He filed an appeal of that ruling, but it was dismissed this past August because he failed to move it forward.
He is also on the hook for millions of dollars in default judgments against him obtained by former clients of his firm, though has said he will contest them.
His attempt to overturn one of those judgments, for $500,000, was rejected by the Ontario Court of Appeal in February.
Defendant dismissed his criminal lawyer

Cartel hired veteran criminal lawyer Richard Posner to defend him late last year, but split with Posner 4½ months later amid a dispute over his fees and trial strategy, according to records obtained by CBC from a separate case in which Cartel challenged Posner's billings.

Those records show Cartel wanted his lawyer to try to get his charge dismissed as an abuse of process — a rare remedy available when a defendant can show that the prosecution's conduct seriously compromised the accused's right to a fair trial.
"In my respectful view, there is no basis for advancing an abuse of process claim in this case," Posner emailed Cartel, according to documents from their fee dispute.
"If you want to bring this motion, you will need to discharge me and find another lawyer or represent yourself."

items: Lawyer couple accused of stealing millions from homebuyers while law society stalled
Lawyers at centre of $7M real estate embezzlement case charged with fraud

blocks.text: At another point, Cartel and Posner differed over whether they should agree at trial to certain of the prosecution's alleged facts.
"Why dispute or make the Crown prove things that are plain and obvious from the business records? In my view, it makes no sense to do so, but the choice is yours," Posner wrote to Cartel.

Ultimately, Posner wrote to Cartel in April of this year: "Based on the tenor and content of your email, along with your previous communications with the members of my office, it is my respectful view there has been a breakdown in our solicitor-client relationship. Accordingly, I will be requesting to be removed from the record on the next court date."
Cartel replied: "I was going to terminate your services Monday, in any event…. I have long ago lost any faith that you or your firm could represent my best interests."

items: Toronto lawyer couple sentenced to jail for contempt over millions in missing homebuyer funds
Lawyer who admitted stealing millions of dollars from homeowners is disbarred

blocks.text: Cartel told CBC News on Monday, on the sidelines of his trial, that he and Posner had settled their dispute out of court.

He is representing himself in his criminal trial. The judge, Rachel Grinburg, referred to that fact in court several times Monday, emphasizing that she wanted to ensure the proceedings were fair to him.

His law licence has been provisionally suspended since April 2024 by the Law Society of Ontario, which has levelled 20 disciplinary accusations against him, including 12 counts of misappropriation of client funds.
Bui was disbarred by the Law Society in December.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Zach Dubinsky is a CBC investigative journalist. His reporting on offshore tax havens (including the Paradise Papers and Panama Papers), political corruption and organized crime has won multiple national and international awards. articles.title: US judge blocks Trump policy of fining migrants up to $1.8 million
articles.summary: As recently as July, the Department of Homeland Security said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants amounting to about $84 billion in total since President Trump returned to the White…

blocks.text: INJUNCTION ORDER. A US judge blocks an order to detain British national Imran Ahmed, CEO of the Center for Countering Digital Hate
Dado Ruvic/Reuters

As recently as July, the Department of Homeland Security said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants amounting to about $84 billion in total since President Trump returned to the White House in 2024

items: A federal judge blocked the Trump administration's attempt to impose fines on migrants who do not leave the US after deportation orders, ruling the fines were unlawful.
US District Judge George O'Toole stated that collecting these fines could lead to insolvency for the affected migrants, who are already in precarious economic situations.
The ruling came in response to a class-action lawsuit challenging the legality of the fines and the process by which they were imposed, which lacked proper public comment and specific allegations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
A federal judge on Monday, October 5, blocked efforts by the Trump administration to impose fines of up to $1.8 million on migrants who fail to leave the US after receiving final deportation orders.

US District Judge George O’Toole in Boston issued the ruling in a class-action lawsuit filed last year by two of the thousands of migrants who have been assessed civil penalties by the Department of Homeland Security.

He said the administration imposed the fines unlawfully. Halting the penalty-related policies was necessary, O’Toole said, because collecting the fines would likely drive the plaintiffs into insolvency.
“The plaintiffs live in an economically precarious position even without the imposition of the government’s exorbitant fines,” he wrote.
DHS had no immediate comment.
As recently as July, the department said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants amounting to about $84 billion in total since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.
While Congress authorized civil penalties under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, no administration sought to impose them until Trump’s first term.

Starting last year, Trump’s second administration began levying fines of $998 per day for migrants who failed to leave the US after a deportation order. Those fines have been imposed retroactively for up to five years, for a maximum penalty of $1.8 million.

In July 2025, DHS and the US Department of Justice implemented a new process they said would streamline the assessment of fines by eliminating a 30-day notice period and shortening the process for challenging penalties.

The plaintiffs, who also included the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, challenged that policy as well as what they described as a practice by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a DHS agency, of issuing fines using boilerplate forms without independently assessing whether someone’s failure to depart was “willful” or “voluntary.”

O’Toole, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, sided with the plaintiffs, holding that the fines were unlawful and violated the Administrative Procedure Act because the forms lacked specific allegations explaining why an individual’s conduct warranted a penalty.

He also found the administration had failed to comply with rulemaking processes in adopting its streamlined fine-imposition process because it did not provide the public a chance to comment on the policy change first. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Measles cases are spreading in the US this year, with over 1,000 infections reported in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: A measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has topped 1,000 cases, with neighboring New York declaring a disaster emergency and mobilizing measures to fight the spread.

image.caption: A child receives a measles vaccine during an outbreak in Texas last year [FILE: Feb 27, 2025]Image: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Over 1,000 cases of measles have been recorded so far this year in Pennsylvania alone, health officials in the northeastern US state said on Monday, the largest outbreak in a US state since the early 1990s.
The US Center for Disease Control (CDC) has put the number of cases recorded nationwide so far this year at 3,869, in what is seen as the worst year for measles since 1991.
What do we know about the latest measles outbreak?

The current outbreak started west of Philadelphia in April, health officials said. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five have died. Nearly all of the cases involved people who were not vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
In neighboring New York on Monday, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a month-long state disaster emergency to "strengthen ongoing efforts to confront" measles.
Over 100 cases have been recorded this year in New York State outside of New York City, with 92 of those reported in "under-immunized" rural areas since July 15.
The executive order suspends regulations on administering vaccines, expanding permission to paramedics and midwives, while allowing nurses to order testing and lowering permission barriers.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said.
US vaccine coverage dips
Since last year, measles has broken out in several US states, including Texas, Utah and South Carolina, which has reported just under 1,000 cases.
Measles includes symptoms like high fever, cough, and rash. It can cause serious complications, especially in young children. It is highly contagious but can be prevented with vaccines.
However, skepticism toward vaccines in the US has risen in recent years, with more parents waiving routine vaccinations amid disinformation about vaccine safety.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?
In 2000, the US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles with high vaccination rates, but coverage has recently dipped below the 95% necessary to prevent outbreaks.

US Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, who has expressed views skeptical of vaccines that are not backed by science, has characterized vaccinations as a "personal choice."

Although Kennedy maintains that the measles vaccine is the best defense against the highly contagious and potentially fatal infection, he has also advocated unproven "alternative treatments" like taking vitamins.

articles.title: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
articles.summary:
Nidal Hasan sentenced to death by military jury in 2013 for carrying out deadly shooting attack at army base in Texas

Donald Trump has approved the execution by US army firing squad of Nidal…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has approved the execution by US army firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a social media post.
Hasan, who was an army psychiatrist, would become first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.

Parnell said in a post on X that defense secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan”.
He added: “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.”
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base.

He chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.

Hasan, a US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on 5 November 2009 at a medical facility in the sprawling military base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.

The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that Hasan had spoken online with the radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an al-Qaida propagandist and American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
Although US mass shootings are disturbingly common, they are rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.
A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group.”
Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital before being shot dead by officers.

articles.title: Sergeant found not guilty of assaulting military police officers who removed her from 17 Wing
articles.summary: A Royal Canadian Air Force sergeant who refused to leave a restricted area of Winnipeg's 17 Wing has been found not guilty of assaulting the military police officers who had removed her from the base…

image.caption: Sgt. Athena Morris has been found not guilty of assaulting three members of the military police at 17 Wing in Winnipeg. The decision was handed down by military Judge Col. Stephen Strickey at HMCS Chippawa on Monday. (Santiago Arias Orozco/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A Royal Canadian Air Force sergeant who refused to leave a restricted area of Winnipeg's 17 Wing has been found not guilty of assaulting the military police officers who had removed her from the base using what a martial court ruled involved the use of excessive force.
Sgt. Athena Morris intended to bring attention to important issue but showed lack of judgment, judge ruled
However, Sgt. Athena Morris has been ordered to pay a fine for unlawfully entering the space to conduct a "peaceful protest" that required police intervention.

"Your intent was to bring attention to an important issue that affected you personally," military Judge Col. Stephen Strickey said Monday before a court martial held at HMCS Chippawa, a Royal Canadian Navy reserve division in Winnipeg.
"However, as a senior non-commissioned member of the CAF with 20 years of service … this was a regrettable lack of judgment on your part."

Court has heard that Morris jumped over a service counter and, using a scarf, tied herself to a chair in an administrative space that was off-limits to the public, known as the orderly room, after she was denied a request to change her gender marker on the Canadian Armed Forces' national human resources records system on March 31, 2025.
Three military police officers repeatedly asked her to leave, but Morris said she wouldn't do it until her information was updated, according to an agreed statement of circumstances read Monday.

The officers handcuffed Morris and placed her in the back of a cruiser where she was shocked with an energy conductive weapon. She was charged with assaulting a police officer and with resisting or escaping from arrest or custody.
Police conduct doesn't excuse sergeant's actions: prosecutor

Morris filed an application alleging her Charter rights were infringed during the arrest. The court found the military police had used excessive force and failed to provide reasonable assistance to facilitate her access to counsel while she was in hospital.
The court determined a sentence reduction was the "appropriate remedy" in light of the Charter breaches.

Maj. Laurent Carignan told court the prosecution accepted the ruling and on Monday they didn't present evidence on the three separate counts Morris initially faced for allegedly assaulting a police officer — so she was found not guilty.
The Charter violation was also an "essential component" to a joint recommendation by the prosecution and defence to sentence Morris to a $2,000 fine, Carignan said.

Morris pleaded guilty to entering a restricted administrative workspace on the base without authorization and refusing to leave until she was removed. Under the National Defence Act, the offence could carry a maximum punishment of dismissal from the Canadian Armed Forces with disgrace, according to the judge.
Carignan said Morris's misconduct does not excuse the "unconstitutional conduct" of the military police, but it also doesn't erase the seriousness of her actions.

"Her chosen conduct was serious," Carignan told court. "The prosecution recognizes the administrative issue was important and deeply personal to her. But its importance did not authorize her to enter a restricted workplace and remain there until she was forcibly removed."
'Ongoing pattern of discrimination': Morris

Morris told the court martial the events leading up to her arrest didn't occur in isolation, but against a broader backdrop of ongoing disputes concerning her gender identity transition within the Armed Forces.

The sergeant said she had been ordered to stop using the women's washroom and instead use the men's shower facility. Morris said the CAF declined to update her email address with her preferred name and when she went to the orderly room to have her gender marker corrected, it had already been at least four months of attempting to get it changed.
"I understood it in the context of what I had already experienced … an ongoing pattern of discrimination," she told court.
The issues continued following her arrest, Morris said. She was misgendered and called by her dead name in written communication, even after providing legal documentation with her new name, she said.

"What has caused much of the lasting harm has been the experience of identifying a problem, explaining why it was discriminatory or harmful, and then finding that the institutions or individuals involved were unwilling to reconsider their position," Morris said.
Defence counsel Maj. Carlos Da Cruz told court Morris's actions were not a random act of indiscipline, but an incident born of sheer exhaustion and desperation — without violence or threat of it.

"She was backed into a corner by a failure at the very institution tasked with assisting her," he said. "Her moral blameworthiness must be heavily mitigated by the fact that she was reacting to a persistent systemic failure to respect her human dignity."
Da Cruz said Morris has an otherwise clean record, filled with military accomplishments, and she did not consider the impact her actions had on the operations at the administrative space.

items: Sergeant tied herself to chair at Winnipeg's air force base after bid to change gender in records denied

blocks.text: But the prosecution argued Morris's behavior already had a "significant sustained negative impacts" on operations across multiple units — resorting to new protocols such as installing physical barriers and alarm systems in customer service areas.
"Military service demands self-discipline, emotional control, some judgment and professional conflict resolution. On this occasion, Sgt. Morris did not demonstrate those qualities," Naurent said.
Strickey said he agrees that a CAF member cannot respond in the way Morris did to an administrative area, regardless of the issue's importance.
The judge also said the focus on the sentence should be placed to deter other offenders from committing similar acts and acknowledged the harm done to the community.
"A fine of $2,000 would represent a meaningful sanction," Strickey's decision said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Santiago Arias Orozco is a journalist with CBC Manitoba currently based in Winnipeg. He previously worked for CBC Toronto and the Toronto Star. You can reach him at santiago.arias.orozco@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations
articles.summary: Hall housing Michael Kotlikoff’s office spray painted as demonstrators demand resignation of college president
articles.byline: Sam Levin, Keely Aouga and Edward Helmore

blocks.text: Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.

Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.

Protesters shouted, “Ban the frats” and held signs saying, “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting, “Kotlikoff, resign!”

The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president’s office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators listen to a speaker during a protest on 5 October 2026, in Ithaca, New York. Photograph: Adrian Kraus/AP

blocks.text: The messages in red paint read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED”. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting “the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”.

“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added. The students’ painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.

blocks.caption: People attend a Justice for Survivors rally at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Photograph: Lauren Petracca/Reuters

blocks.text: “We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”

The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”

The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe’s case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of Cornell students participate in a rally against the university’s actions. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.

A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.

One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said: “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”

blocks.caption: Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against Cornell University’s handling of the 2024 fraternity-house gang rape allegations. Photograph: Adrian Kraus/AP

blocks.text: Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office’s handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe’s attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.
Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.

Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

items: The Department of Agriculture assures the public of sufficient food supply amid Super El Niño, with a P45 billion fund for fertilizer assistance.
Current food supply days are reported as 75 days for rice, 125 days for chicken, 170 days for pork, and 90 days for corn, with no immediate cause for panic.

Progressive lawmakers are calling for an investigation into the impact of Super El Niño on agriculture, while additional funds and preparations are being made for the anticipated worsening effects next year.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Agriculture (DA) assured the public that the food supply is sufficient to tide over the effects of Super El Niño, and that it has secured P45 billion in fertilizer assistance for farmers and fisherfolk.

“[I]n general, I would just like to state that we are maintaining a healthy number of days of food sufficiency,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said during a Malacañang briefing on Monday, October 5.
Tiu Laurel gave a breakdown of the current supply as of Monday:

items: Rice: 75 days
Chicken: 125 days
Pork: 170 days
Corn: 90 days

blocks.text: “If we are able to maintain this, there’s no reason to panic actually,” said Tiu Laurel. The agriculture chief said he has directed the National Food Authority to fill their warehouses with local rice. Importations will be government’s “last resort.”

blocks.caption: Food supply sufficient for Super El Niño, P45-B aid coming for farmers – DA

blocks.text: Progressive lawmakers in the House of Representatives are seeking an investigation into the impact of Super El Niño to farmers, fisherfolk, and the government’s preparations to protect the hardest-hit sectors.

Billions of pesos are earmarked for the agriculture sector. The DA now has P6.2 billion out of their P45-billion fund request to provide fuel and fertilizer aid. Another P10 billion from this request would be for solar irrigations, solar pumps, solar aerators, and additional fertilizer.
More funds are coming next year, when the effects of El Niño are expected to worsen.

“For 2027, we have added P10 billion through the help of Congress for the presidential assistance for farmers and fisherfolk in anticipation of the problems from El Niño,” said Tiu Laurel in a mix of Filipino and English.

The government has advised the public against hoarding food products. The environment department said there is no cause yet to declare a climate emergency but that they are directed to “prepare for the worst-case scenario.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Inflation soars to 7.2% as food, fuel prices climb in September 2026
articles.summary: The latest surge in inflation marks the end of a disinflation trend that brought the rate down for four straight months from the 7.2% also recorded in April

blocks.text: MARKET. People buy basic commodities at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.
Rappler
The latest surge in inflation marks the end of a disinflation trend that brought the rate down for four straight months from the 7.2% also recorded in April

items: Headline inflation in the Philippines rose to 7.2% in September, driven by bad weather affecting food prices and higher fuel costs.
The average inflation from January to September was 5.4%.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Inflation accelerated in September as bad weather pushed up food prices while higher fuel costs and a weaker peso added to price pressures.

Headline inflation rose to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported on Tuesday, October 6. This matched the three-year high of 7.2% in April and marked the end of four straight months of decline.
Average inflation from January to September stood at 5.4%, remaining well above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%.
The September figure fell within the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) forecast range of 6.4% to 7.4%.

Ahead of the release, the BSP had warned that weather disturbances could push up prices of vegetables, fish, rice, and fruits, adding inflationary pressure. Higher domestic petroleum prices and the peso’s depreciation were also expected to add to inflation.

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. had forecast inflation at 6.9%. Neri said monsoon rain and flooding disrupted the supply and transport of perishable food, while a series of fuel price hikes in the second half of September wiped out the relief from earlier rollbacks.

He warned that September could mark the beginning of another inflation upswing, with price growth potentially exceeding 7% in the coming months. Unlike the April spike, which was heavily influenced by fuel, BPI expects the next wave to be “broader and stickier, driven by food, labor costs, and more.”

The full impact of fare increases that took effect on September 28 will also only be felt from October onwards, with other upside risks including the Middle East tensions, the pending decision on Meralco’s rate reset that could lead to higher electricity rates, and the peso’s continued weakness.
Manulife Investment Philippines said the BSP should continue focusing on keeping inflation expectations anchored rather than reacting primarily to short-term peso movements.
Jean Olivia de Castro, Manulife Investment Philippines’ head of fixed income, noted that much of the currency’s weakness is driven by elevated US treasury yields and broad dollar strength.
The BSP raised its key policy rate to 5% in August, its third consecutive 25-basis-point increase. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump says Super Pac will pay for taxpayer-funded ads that sparked outcry
articles.summary:
President’s U-turn comes after Democrats and Republicans condemned use of tax dollars for pro-Trump ads

Donald Trump said on Monday he would pay for taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads “with…

blocks.text: Donald Trump said on Monday he would pay for taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads “with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”, a political action committee, after the television advertisements glorifying himself sparked a major backlash.
In a social media post, Trump characterized the ads, which cost at least $1.5m in federal funds, as “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” and called them “a rather standard thing to do”.
Maga Inc is Trump’s political war chest, which had amassed more than $400m by the end of July. Trump has begun to tap it to boost Republican candidates across the US ahead of midterm elections.
Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such advertising.

The White House – which had fiercely defended using taxpayer money on spots meant to promote the president – said Monday night Maga Inc would pay for such ads in the future. It did not answer questions on how it or Trump might prove that his political funds were being used on any ads.
Trump’s abrupt about-face came after leaders from both parties criticized using taxpayer funds.

Last week, two congressional Democrats asked federal watchdogs to investigate whether the Trump administration illegally used taxpayer money to air the television spots that began airing in late September.

Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, and California congressman George Whitesides wrote to the government accountability office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC), describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”.

Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for “publicity or propaganda” and one limiting the partisan political activities of government employees.

The first ad featured clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history”, “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police”.

Later the same week, a second ad began running. It showed scenic videos of Mount Rushmore with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary.

A third, more recent one was virtually identical to an ad for Trump’s Republican reelection campaign in 2024 and showed him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers”.
All ended with a message: “Paid for by the US government.”

According to AdImpact, which tracks media spending, the spots had cost at least $1.4m by the end of September. The actual amount spent could be far more, depending on whether networks classified the ad as a political ad.

articles.title: Did a Russian lab worker die from pneumonic plague? What we know — and don't know
articles.summary: An unnerving story has emerged from southeastern Russia involving the death of 28-year-old woman from pneumonia and fears that she may have been exposed to a form of plague at the lab where she…

image.caption: A view of the Medical Assistance and Rescue Centre, an infectious diseases hospital, in the town of Shelekhov in the Irkutsk region of Russia, on Oct. 5. (Stringer/Reuters)

blocks.text: Nearly 200 quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies

An unnerving story has emerged from southeastern Russia involving the death of 28-year-old woman from pneumonia and fears that she may have been exposed to a form of plague at the lab where she worked.
Yes, plague — specifically, pneumonic plague.

Few details are confirmed. Russian authorities say there is currently no evidence that the illness was connected to any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
But the governor of a neighbouring region fuelled speculation over the weekend when he posted on Telegram suggesting the woman had died of plague, later altering his comment to include "maybe."

People have been quarantined at the hospital where she died last week; many others who came in contact with her were put under medical supervision, according to Anna Popova, Russia's public health agency.

There are, however, questions about Russian authorities' transparency, along with general shock at the thought of someone dying from an illness associated with the Middle Ages — and that many don't realize still exists.
Here's what we know and what we don't know about the situation in the Siberian city of Irkutsk, the lab worker who died and what Russian and other global officials are saying about the case.
What happened?
Russian state-run news agency TASS reported that the employee was "diagnosed with pneumonia of unknown etiology."
Local media reports have identified her as laboratory technician Darya Shipilova, saying she died on Friday.

The lab, which was established under the former Soviet Union in 1934, carries out scientific research on plague control, vaccine development and epidemic prevention, as well as work on other dangerous infectious diseases like cholera, brucellosis and anthrax.
CBC News has not independently confirmed Shipilova's identity or details about her work.

items: At 'crucial' moment for pandemic preparedness, experts say world isn't ready

blocks.text: Russian-language reports say that Shipilova went to a hospital in Shelekhov, about 20 kilometres southwest of Irkutsk, days before her death.

Per Ria Novosti, another state-run outlet, Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev announced on Friday that a resident had been diagnosed with a "a particularly dangerous infection" of an undetermined nature.
"Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified," Kobzev said.
What is pneumonic plague?

Plague, which came to be known as the Black Death when it ravaged Europe in the 1300s, is an infectious disease caused by a bacterium known as Yersinia pestis, or Y. pestis. It is carried by small mammals and generally spread by the fleas that feed off them.
Those fleas can transmit Y. pestis to humans and other large mammals.
There are three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague, the most common form, causes buboes — painful, inflammed lymph nodes near the site of a flea bite. Symptoms usually come on after three to seven days, and can include fever, chills, headache and extreme exhaustion.

Septicemic plague happens when bubonic plague infections aren't treated and spread to the bloodstream and other parts of the body. It can cause vomiting, diarrhea, multiple organ failures and septic shock.
Pneumonic plague is when Y. pestis infects the lungs, making it much more of a risk because it can then be transmitted between people through airborne droplets.
Symptoms — including high fever, cough, coughing up blood and difficulty breathing — can occur within one to three days of inhalation. It can be fatal if left untreated.
How deadly is it?
Plague is easily treated with antibiotics, which did not exist during the Black Death, Dr. Malick Gibani, a clinical associate professor at Imperial College London, told CBC News.
But people do still die from it, he says, though that's generally restricted to certain geographic areas, often due to conditions that attract rodents, or the fact that they are remote.

Between 2019 and 2025, the World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 3,847 suspected cases and 423 deaths in 10 countries. Most of those infections occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.
In 2017, a pneumonic plague outbreak in the latter country affected more than 2,400 people and killed 209 people.
But Gibani notes that plague infections can occur in other parts of the world like parts of Russia, as well as in South America and and parts of the western U.S.
Siberia was the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak of plague.
Do I need to be worried?

While there are still many unanswered questions, this possible outbreak is nothing like the COVID-19 pandemic because plague is "a much different pathogen," said Angela Rasmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan.
Even before they become sick, infected people are "constantly shedding" the virus that causes COVID-19, she said, which is how it spread so far.
"You're not going to be walking around feeling fine, shedding Yersinia pestis everywhere for everybody else to breathe in," she said.

items: Inside the Montreal lab preparing Canada for the next pandemic

blocks.text: In fact, you should be more concerned about coming into contact with an infected rodent than getting an infection potentially from a lab in Siberia, she says.
Even though it's not been officially confirmed that Shipilova died of pneumonic plague, Gibani says a rapid response is key to controlling the spread in any situation like this.
He says that can include contact tracing and offering antibiotics to those who may have been identified as being at risk of exposure.
LISTEN | Where scientists believe they found ground zero for 'Black Death':
Quirks and Quarks8:08The Black Death was history’s most lethal plague. Now we know where it started
How is the rest of the world reacting?
Russian officials have sought to quell fears about a possible outbreak.

But some countries, such as Kazakhstan, aren't taking chances and are raising alerts or implementing quarantine at border crossings. Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan have implemented similar measures even though they don't share borders with Russia.
The WHO is in contact Russian health authorities and has offered support if needed, a spokesperson said in a statement to CBC News.

items: Earliest outbreak of the plague killed hunter-gatherer kids 5,500 years ago

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump also said his administration would also offer assistance.

"Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to Nebraska, calling the possible outbreak a "big problem for Russia."
Health Canada told CBC it is also monitoring the situation, though it sees no risk to Canada at this time. According to the agency, the last recorded human case of plague in this country was in 1939.

articles.title: China accuses PH aircraft of ‘illegal’ intrusion over Bajo de Masinloc
articles.summary: China warned Manila against “provocative acts” in the disputed West Philippine Sea after accusing a Philippine military aircraft of illegally entering the airspace over Bajo de Masinloc…

blocks.text: A Philippine C-208 aircraft and a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft encounter each other over the vicinity of Bajo de Masinloc on Oct. 3, 2026.
Chinese Embassy in Manila via Facebook / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — China warned Manila against “provocative acts” in the disputed West Philippine Sea after accusing a Philippine military aircraft of illegally entering the airspace over Bajo de Masinloc on October 3.

The warning came after the Armed Forces of the Philippines said a Chinese J-16 fighter repeatedly made close maneuvers around a Philippine C-208 aircraft conducting a routine maritime patrol near the disputed shoal.

Senior Capt. Zhai Shichen, spokesperson for the People's Liberation Army Southern Theater Command, said the Philippine aircraft “illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's Huangyan Dao,” Beijing's name for Bajo de Masinloc.
China claims most of the South China Sea, including Bajo de Masinloc, despite a 2016 international arbitral ruling that rejected the legal basis of Beijing's expansive claims in the waterway.
Zhai said Chinese naval and air forces tracked and monitored the Philippine aircraft and issued warnings to expel it “in accordance with laws and regulations.”

“The Philippine side seriously violate China’s sovereignty and are highly likely to cause unintended maritime and air incidents,” Zhai said in a statement shared on social media and posted by the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines on Facebook.
He warned Manila to stop what China described as “rights-violation and provocative acts.”
“Forces of the STC remain on high alert at all times to firmly safeguard national sovereignty and security as well as regional peace and stability,” Zhai said.
AFP reports close encounter
The AFP, however, gave a different account of the incident.
In a statement issued Sunday, the military said its C-208 aircraft was conducting a routine maritime patrol near Bajo de Masinloc when it encountered two Chinese military aircraft.
One of them was identified as a J-16 fighter.

The Chinese fighter repeatedly approached and maneuvered in close proximity to the Philippine aircraft, including moving ahead of and around it and positioning itself within the C-208's wake, according to the AFP.
“These maneuvers posed an aviation safety risk,” the military said.
The AFP described the incident as part of a recurring pattern of “unsafe and coercive behavior” against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations.
The Philippine aircrew remained professional and exercised due caution in accordance with established aviation procedures, the AFP said.
The C-208 completed its assigned maritime patrol and returned safely without further incident.
Bajo de Masinloc, also known as Scarborough Shoal, lies about 124 nautical miles off Zambales and has remained a major flashpoint between Manila and Beijing in the West Philippine Sea.
More encounters reported
The Philippine government also reported a second confrontation on Sunday in the Spratly Islands, farther south in the South China Sea.
The weekend incidents came about two weeks after the Philippines said a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine fisheries department boat in another part of the Spratlys.
China subsequently blamed the Philippine vessel for that incident, saying it “bears full responsibility.”
Tensions between Manila and Beijing have remained high as both sides continue to assert competing claims in the South China Sea.

articles.title: Ottawa plans Crown corporation to break defence procurement logjam
articles.summary: The Liberal government plans to transform its year-old Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation, giving it greater independence and potentially sweeping powers to accelerate military…

image.caption: Doug Guzman, CEO of the Defence Investment Agency, left, listens as Prime Minister Mark Carney takes questions from journalists at the Canadian Association of Defence and Security Industries annual defence industry trade show on May 27. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Liberal government plans to transform its year-old Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation, giving it greater independence and potentially sweeping powers to accelerate military purchases. The proposed overhaul could fundamentally reshape Canada's notoriously cumbersome defence procurement system, while raising fresh questions about oversight, accountability and how far Ottawa will go.
Legislation expected to transform Defence Investment Agency into independent body
The Liberal government plans to turn the fledgling Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation in order to move military purchases along more swiftly, two federal sources tell CBC News.
The move will potentially give Ottawa substantially more freedom to run defence procurement like a specialized commercial enterprise rather than as a conventional government program.
The confidential sources, who were not authorized to speak publicly, said it's expected the Crown corporation would report to an associate minister of defence for public accountability purposes.

The DIA was created just over a year ago and has functioned as a special agency under Public Services and Procurement Canada. Legislation giving the defence agency broader powers to bypass the decades-old procurement system was put before the House of Commons in the spring and has yet to pass.

However, Public Works Minister Joël Lightbound plans on introducing new, separate legislation taking the DIA one step further into independent Crown corporation status. The title of the proposed bill has appeared in House of Commons documents.

Many defence experts agree the biggest advantage to making the agency a Crown corporation is operational independence. While details of the new legislation haven't been released, it's expected the agency could have its own board, CEO, corporate plan and workforce.
For the Canadian Armed Forces, the attraction of dealing with a Crown corporation for its equipment rests in the possibility that what it orders could arrive faster.
Prime Minister Mark Carney made speeding up defence procurement an important campaign promise in the 2025 election.
When the first bill to formally create the DIA was tabled earlier this year it gave the new agency sweeping powers.
For decades, the federal government could use four exceptions to suspend the normal procurement process.
In the spring, the government proposed to allow up to 14 exceptions, including procurements of national interest. It also made economic security a key pillar of the DIA mandate.
How those measures will be reflected in the Crown corporation and whether it will have even greater authority is unclear.
Both Defence Minister David McGuinty and Secretary of State for Defence Procurement Stephen Fuhr are scheduled to hold a media availability on Tuesday to answer questions.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: LIVE: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Oct. 6
articles.summary: The Senate resumes Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 6, with Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura set to return to the witness…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate resumes Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 6, with Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura set to return to the witness stand.
Buenaventura will continue his cross-examination by the defense panel in connection with Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which accuses Duterte of accumulating unexplained wealth.
The prosecution and defense will be given the opportunity for redirect and recross examinations after the defense completes its questioning.
Senator-judges will then be allowed to ask questions or make interjections.
On Monday, the Senate impeachment court allowed Buenaventura to testify on the bank transactions of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Buenaventura said at least P4.4 billion in covered and suspicious transactions were recorded under the bank accounts of Duterte and Carpio. Of this amount, P1.63 billion were inflows, while P1.3 billion were outflows. Another P1.4 billion involved transactions with undetermined inflows and outflows.
He also confirmed that Cale88 Foods Corp., a company linked to Carpio, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
Watch the continuation of the impeachment trial today at 10 a.m.

articles.title: Senator-judges call out defense over ‘threats’ on AMLA records disclosure
articles.summary: Senator-judges of the impeachment court called out the defense panel for what they called veiled threats of criminal liability directed at the witness, the media and potentially the court itself over…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judges of the impeachment court called out the defense panel for what they called veiled threats of criminal liability directed at the witness, the media and potentially the court itself over the disclosure of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records.

This was after defense counsel Mark Vinluan on Monday, October 5, repeatedly asked witness AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura about the strict confidentiality provisions of Sections 8A and 9C of the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA).

Vinluan, during his cross-examination of Buenaventura, even read the penal provisions of Section 14 of the law aloud, highlighting that unauthorized disclosures of confidential information carry prison terms of three to eight years, hefty fines, and absolute perpetual disqualification from public office for public officials.
He also pointedly noted that under Section 9C, members of the media who publish or report such confidential transactions could be held criminally liable.
Vinluan’s line of questioning did not sit well with several senator-judges, who accused the defense of attempting to intimidate the witness and silence the press.
Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo was the first to openly express his frustration, calling out the defense for repeatedly badgering the witness, who had been on the stand since 10:00 a.m.

"I can see this defense is repeatedly badgering the witness... and I don't see any reason why the defense is repeatedly threatening him, even threatening the media, mentioning the P500,000 [fine]," Tulfo said.
"We already ruled earlier that the disclosure of AMLA records is allowed in this impeachment court... Give us a break, okay?"

Following Tulfo, Senator-judge Kiko Pangilinan also raised concerns regarding the defense counsel's repeated emphasis on potential criminal liability for disclosing AMLA records, noting that the witness had already clarified that his disclosure was authorized pursuant to a subpoena.

Pangilinan also pointed out that the defense had similarly questioned the House prosecution over the disclosure of AMLA records during House proceedings, expressing concern that the defense might also attempt to raise the issue of possible criminal liability against senator-judges during cross-examination.

“If the defense wishes to raise this issue, bring it to the Supreme Court perhaps. But raising the issue of possible criminal liability for authorized disclosure in this impeachment court, I believe, isn't called for,” Pangilinan said.
Senator-judge Vicente Sotto III reminded the courtroom of the constitutional protections afforded to the legislature.
"The counsels in the impeachment board should be reminded of the term parliamentary immunity," Sotto said.
Senator-Judge Risa Hontiveros strongly echoed Tulfo’s sentiments, defending the role of the press in covering the impeachment trial.
“Tingin ko rin po mali rin na kahit indirectly bantaan ng media sa pagganap nila ng kanilang essential na tungkulin na i-cover 'yung mga proceedings na ito,” Hontiveros said.
(I think it is wrong to even indirectly threaten the media in the performance of their essential duty to cover these proceedings.)
“Dapat po walang chilling effect na either sa sadya or 'di sadya na lilikhain sa hanay ng fourth estate,” she added.
(There should be no chilling effect, whether intentional or unintentional, created within the ranks of the Fourth Estate.)

Vinluan’s questions during his cross-examination came after the prosecution team, through lawyer Mae Divinagracia, asked Buenaventura about details of several bank transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte that involved foreign currency.
This drew opposition from the defense panel and some senator-judges, citing confidentiality clauses under the AMLA.

However, Senate presiding officer Francis Escudero allowed the discussion of its details, citing Supreme Court rulings that say that the AMLC cannot invoke confidentiality clauses under the AMLA to prevent disclosure of information on covered and suspicious transaction reports.

articles.title: Oil from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers

Oil is being shipped from South Korea to…

blocks.text: Oil is being shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.

Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.

“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Seoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.

But South Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.

While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.

The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyiv come under strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.

The largest carrier, the sanctioned Layla, made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.

Another sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flagged Astoria, which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.

The third sanctioned tanker, the Chongchon, never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I, at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.
The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.

Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.

According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions, and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.

In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.
Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.
In March, as the war with Iran shut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.
On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.

When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”

It said it had expanded its export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.
The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.
The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.

A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”

articles.title: A simple guide to the US midterms
articles.summary: US voters will head to the polls on 3 November in a ballot that could have a major impact on Donald Trump’s presidency.

blocks.text: There are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
What are the midterms?
On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.
A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.
The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.
The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.
Who is being elected?
All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is where proposed laws are introduced and debated.

Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House.
On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched.
What are the key issues?
The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare.
Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.
Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs have also pushed up prices for Americans.

Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration.

Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology.
What is at stake?
Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation.

Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats and the minimum needed for control is 51.
If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.
Who might win?
Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them.

Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him.
But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats.
The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified nine Senate races to watch, external, in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio.
The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn.
Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Josh Turek (Democrat) and Ashley Hinson (Republican) are in a tight race for Iowa's Senate seat

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Josh Turek (Democrat) and Ashley Hinson (Republican) are in a tight race for Iowa's Senate seat
What does it mean for Trump?
If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress.
So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party.

Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny.
There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial.
If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office.
What does it mean for the 2028 election?
The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far.
Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership.

Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats.
