articles.title: NDRRMC: State of calamity declared in 106 areas due to El Niño
articles.summary: State of calamity was declared in 106 areas as dry conditions driven by the El Niño phenomenon continue to intensify across the country.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 7:25am
State of calamity was declared in 106 areas as dry conditions driven by the El Niño phenomenon continue to intensify across the country.
In its report on Monday, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) said these areas are in five regions:

items: Cagayan Valley - 66
Calabarzon - 4
Bicol - 12
Soccsksargen - 1
Caraga - 23

blocks.text: At least 39 wild, forest, and mountain fire incidents were recorded in Caraga Administrative Region.
Four cities and municipalities reported water supply interruptions, while 33 localities were forced to suspend classes in the region.
Across the country, the NDRRMC reported that 104,149 families or 388,375 individuals have been affected by El Niño, particularly in Cagayan Valley, Bicol, Calabarzon, and Caraga.
Agricultural damage and production losses were estimated at P5.56 billion, according to the NDRRMC. Cagayan Valley accounted for the majority of agricultural destruction with P4.96 billion.
A total of 201,322 farmers and fisherfolk have been affected nationwide, with over 223,497 hectares of crop areas damaged.
Of the total affected farmland, 41,164 hectares suffered total crop loss with no chance of recovery.
Assistance worth P39,058,681 has been provided to affected communities so far, according to the NDRRMC.
On June 9, state weather bureau PAGASA said that indicators confirmed that El Niño conditions were present in the tropical Pacific.
In May 2026, the observed relative sea surface temperature anomaly indicated a warming trend consistent with El Niño development.
El Niño increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall conditions, which may result in adverse impacts such as dry spells and droughts in some areas of the country.
However, over the western part of the country, above-normal rainfall conditions during the Southwest monsoon season may also occur.
On September 23, PAGASA warned of a possibly record-breaking El Niño in the coming months.
Lesser rains are to be expected come October due to the El Niño phenomenon, the state weather bureau said.

PAGASA also said that the El Niño could last until March or even June. Around 40 provinces are expected to experience lesser rainfall during the dry spell and drought. Once January comes, it is expected that this number could leap to 80. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
articles.summary: The city's space boom raises questions about the role of the state in backing important industries.

blocks.text: ByShiona McCallum
Senior technology reporterReporting fromGlasgow

blocks.caption: Shiona McCallum

blocks.text: In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space.

I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde."
What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites.

Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites.

blocks.caption: Image caption, CubeSats - like this one, pictured in the offices of Spire Global in Glasgow - can be used for anything from weather forecasting to global positioning

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
CubeSats - like this one, pictured in the offices of Spire Global in Glasgow - can be used for anything from weather forecasting to global positioning
But crucially, they are modular and can be stacked together, then packed with cameras, sensors, communications equipment or other technology depending on their purpose.

And their size belies their significance. The data collected by satellites of all kinds is increasingly woven into everyday life. It helps us communicate and navigate, track ships and transport goods, monitor forests and crops, manage energy networks and understand changes to our climate.
For governments, that information can help inform decisions and respond to emergencies. As satellites have become more capable, space has become increasingly important.
More than two decades after the first satellite company was established there, the Scottish Government says more small satellites are built in Glasgow than anywhere else in Europe.

Across Scotland, the wider space industry generated £335m in income in 2022-23 - up 69% in five years. Excluding traditional satellite television broadcasting, it employed 2,811 people, an increase of 81% over the same period.
But elsewhere in Europe, governments are committing big money to their own satellite industries.

Could this take investment and jobs away from Glasgow? And if so, what - if anything - should the Scottish and UK governments do about it? And what should be the role of the state when it comes to backing important industries?
Glasgow's rise to small satellite superpower
Perhaps the most surprising thing about Glasgow's success in the space industry is that it wasn't planned.

One of the catalysts was Craig Clark's Clyde Space. The company specialised in CubeSats at just the right moment, a few years after it launched, as smaller and cheaper spacecraft were taking off, and would go on to build Scotland's first satellite, the UKube-1.
Crucially, the tech was built in partnership with the University of Strathclyde - which provided skills and research, as well as a ready supply of engineers.

Other companies followed, including Craft Prospect and Alba Orbital. Expertise grew and a new space cluster began to form. American satellite company Spire chose Glasgow for its European base in 2015. Smaller businesses developed, while established engineering and technology firms became part of the supply chain.
Glasgow: Satellite City
Glasgow has transformed itself into Europe's largest producer of small satellites - but some of the sector's leading figures say Glasgow's position is no longer secure.
Listen now on BBC Sounds.

"Companies started moving to Glasgow because they could see that it was possible to do it here, and there was an ecosystem that was starting to grow," says Andrew Strain, chief technology officer at AAC Clyde Space - the company formed after Clyde Space was acquired by Swedish firm AAC Microtec, although Glasgow remains the group's main satellite manufacturing site.

Soon Glasgow was host to an "entire small satellite value chain", from components and satellite manufacturing, through to launch, spaceports and ground stations, according to Daniel Smith, founder of space marketing firm AstroAgency and the Scottish Government's trade and investment envoy for space.

There are wider benefits too. According to a review commissioned by Space Scotland, space manufacturing alone accounted for more than 1,000 Scottish jobs in 2022-23. The wider industry generated £202m for the Scottish economy.

And as the industry grew, so did the pool of knowledge. There are now more than 100 people working across space-related activity at the University of Strathclyde, with the subject now one of the institution's strategic priorities, according to Prof Malcolm Macdonald, its chair of applied space technology. The university works directly with commercial space companies on research and tech development.

Macdonald recalls that when he graduated, there was basically no local space industry for him to join. Now, "when our graduates leave the university, they will go and work in the local space sector because it is now here in Glasgow for them", he says.
But what's significant, Macdonald says, is that Glasgow's satellite industry wasn't something the government set out to establish. Instead, the process was "largely organic", says Smith.
By any measure it's a success story. But there are warnings about competition from overseas.
"It's not necessarily that we're going backwards," Macdonald tells me. "But other people are catching up."
The challenge to Glasgow

Bavaria is emerging as a significant European hub for aerospace and defence technology. Germany's Defence Ministry says it plans to invest around €35bn (£30bn) in military space capabilities in the coming years, including more than 100 encrypted communications satellites.

For Macdonald, that kind of spending is changing Europe's space industry. Against a backdrop of the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical uncertainty, governments are no longer simply supporting research and innovation. Increasingly, they are becoming major customers rather than just investors.

Will Lecky, co-founder and director of know.space, the space economics consultancy, says that matters because the global playing field is not level. He says UK public space funding falls well behind countries such as France and Germany.
"It's certainly a risk to Glasgow and the wider UK space sector that investment will follow the money and lead to longer term competitive disadvantage as activity flows elsewhere," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Scottish space company Skyrora is celebrating after it says it successfully tested a "hot fire" of its rocket last month

blocks.text: Image source, Skyrora
The Scottish space company Skyrora is celebrating after it says it successfully tested a "hot fire" of its rocket last month

Meanwhile, Finland's aerospace firm ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR), satellites, which can produce images of the Earth's surface through cloud and darkness. Macdonald says these have been used in the war in Ukraine, where satellite imagery can provide intelligence - for example, spotting a Russian vessel in a Crimean port - when conventional optical cameras cannot.
In June, ICEYE announced a funding round worth more than €1bn, valuing the company at more than €10bn. The Finnish state has also increased its stake and now owns around 12% of the company.
Finland's Minister for European Affairs, Joakim Strand, said the geopolitical situation had highlighted the importance of domestic ownership in what he called a "key strategic sector".
Governments want guaranteed access to satellite communications, especially when their country is facing a crisis. Some want the satellites - and the ability to build them - within their own borders.
That can have consequences for Glasgow.
"The recent increases in space spending elsewhere in Europe matter," says Gabriele Piazza, an economist at the London School of Economics who researches government procurement of advanced technology.
Space is not a normal market. Where the contracts go can help determine where companies invest, where engineers work and where expertise builds.
"Since capabilities build on themselves, firms with a large customer at home gain an advantage that lasts," Piazza adds.

Meanwhile, as well as Clyde Space's 2018 acquisition by AAC Microtec, Glasgow-founded Alba Orbital has moved its headquarters to the US, while retaining a Scottish base and team. Spire has expanded its manufacturing operation into Munich.
The Scottish government maintains that Glasgow still builds more small satellites than anywhere else in Europe. So, this is not an industry in decline.
But the bigger challenge, Smith says, is helping companies that start in Scotland to scale here.

"I wouldn't want it to be overly negative," says Macdonald. "It's more just like there are warning lights flashing that other parts of Europe are investing much more aggressively, and moving much more quickly, than we have."
The case for Glasgow staying on top

Satellite camera manufacturer Simera Sense announced this year that it was opening a new production facility in the city, creating 20 highly skilled jobs. The firm, which has premises in South Africa, Belgium and France, will open a high-value electronics assembly lab and office at EastWorks in Dalmarnock.
That suggests something more nuanced than an exodus. Glasgow's concentration of universities, engineers and specialist suppliers, built up over two decades, would be difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Plus, some comparisons with overseas competitors are not exact. ICEYE is just one specialist company focused on radar satellites, while Glasgow is an entire manufacturing cluster producing different kinds of small satellites. Spire expanding in Munich does not necessarily mean it is retreating from Glasgow.
Smith doesn't think the answer is simply trying to outspend competitors: "We can grow alongside them," he says.
Instead, he argues Scotland should focus on what the industry actually needs – filling gaps and helping space companies find customers in areas such as energy, transport and healthcare.
So what role should government play?
With a successful domestic industry facing competition from abroad, you might anticipate calls for the government to provide financial support.

But Lecky cautions against that. He argues Glasgow's small satellite industry originally grew partly because of a lack of government support, as part of the commercially-focused "newspace" revolution.
"We shouldn't jump to government support as being the answer - it's critical to keep this commercial-minded attitude," he says.

"If you offered most entrepreneurs a choice between a grant, with significant paperwork, milestone payments and continuous scrutiny, or a paying customer, I suspect they would always choose the customer," he says.
And increasingly, governments are becoming that customer anyway.
For Smith, government contracts can do something grants cannot - give young companies revenue, a customer and a track record they can use to win business overseas.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Glaswegian engineers say the city will soon have an "end-to-end" space sector

blocks.text: Glaswegian engineers say the city will soon have an "end-to-end" space sector

Piazza says there is an economic case for thinking about procurement too. Building satellites creates knowledge that can spread far beyond the company itself. Engineers move between employers. Suppliers acquire new skills. Ideas become new products - sometimes in entirely different industries.

"Often, tomorrow's industries grow out of today's," he says. "The teams and suppliers building satellites now are the ones able to develop the next generation of a related technology, and once they disperse, they are very hard to reassemble."
But there is a cost.

Piazza points out that money spent supporting one industry cannot be spent on hospitals or schools. Governments can be poor at picking industries. And if everyone subsidises, nobody necessarily gains ground.
That is one reason procurement can make sense. The government buys something it needs anyway. The company gets a customer. Not just a grant.
But that raises a bigger question, made more important by the Ukraine war: what does the UK actually need to be able to do for itself?

Satellites provide communications, navigation and intelligence during conflict. Beyond defence, satellite services underpin parts of transport, energy, telecommunications and emergency response. Governments therefore have to decide which capabilities they are comfortable buying from overseas providers or allies.

Piazza says there can be a strategic case for keeping capabilities that are critical and difficult to replace. He describes it as a form of insurance. But keeping capability at home can mean higher costs, smaller production runs and duplicating what allies already do.

There is evidence that some public investment in space produces significant economic returns. Every £1 of UK investment through the European Space Agency generated £7.49 in direct economic benefit, an independent evaluation commissioned by the UK Space Agency estimated.
The UK Space Agency also says its work helped catalyse £2.2bn in investment and revenue for the UK space sector in 2024-25. But these figures relate to the whole of the UK, not Glasgow specifically.
The more important question may be where the valuable parts of the industry - its people, intellectual property, research and manufacturing - ultimately end up.
"The risk is not closure," says Piazza. "It is that the next phase of growth follows the contracts elsewhere."
Scotland also has another potential addition on the horizon: SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland.
The vision of a fully integrated, "end-to-end" space sector is moving closer to reality. Although the infrastructure is ready, actual launch campaigns have experienced technical delays.
So, success is not guaranteed.
"We are in a great position right now," says Strain. "But if we get complacent, then we can fall behind again because it's moving very, very fast."
Glasgow's shipyards once made the city synonymous with building things for the world. Its space industry has done something similar - almost by accident.
The question now is not whether Glasgow can build a successful satellite industry. It already has.
It is whether the next phase of that success is built here too.

Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura is set to return to the witness stand on Tuesday for the continuation of his cross-examination by the defense panel at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Defense counsel Mark Vinluan is set to continue his questioning of Buenaventura in relation to Article 2 of the impeachment case, alleging that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth.

On Monday, the Senate impeachment court allowed Buenaventura to testify on the bank transactions of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero said that existing provisions in laws on the confidentiality of bank transactions are not absolute because AMLC is not a passive institution to begin with.
Buenaventura disclosed that at least P4.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions were recorded under the bank accounts of Duterte and Carpio.

Of the amount, he said that P1.63 billion accounted for inflows, while P1.3 billion was for outflows. He also said there are P1.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions with undetermined inflows and outflows.

articles.title: Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
articles.summary: The musician received five Oscar nominations, and soundtracked dozens of memorable nature films.

blocks.text: Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76.
The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for The Remains of the Day and Cry Freedom.

His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time.
In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today."
They continued: "He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music."

Fenton was born George Howe in Bromley, Kent in 1949. According to a biography on his official website, his father was a mechanical engineer, and his mother had been a dancer before becoming a nurse during the war.
Both parents were musical - his father played drums and his mother played piano - but Fenton chose the electric guitar as his instrument at the age of seven.
That was "when music became more important than football," he later told The Express newspaper. "The Beatles had a huge influence on me."
He took his first lessons from a musician called Brian Rudd.
"He came into our lives as a chimney sweep, which he clearly wasn't," Fenton later recalled.
"My mother went mad at him because he filled the house with soot.
"As he left he said, 'I'm really sorry – but I tuned the boy's guitar for you.' She suggested that as compensation for the mess he could give me a lesson, which he did and then carried on doing."
Later, Fenton began to study the church organ, but rejected the chance to attend university and music college to pursue a career as a performer.
In 1968, he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play Forty Years On and was forced to adopt his mother's maiden name, as union rules prevented two actors from having the same name.
During that production, he also understudied the musical director of the show, Carl Davis - who similarly became a prominent composer for film and television.
A year later, he signed a record deal, and scored a top 10 hit in Sweden with a cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer, but his career as a solo artist was short lived.
In the mid-1970s, he had a recurring role as soldier Martin Gimbel in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale Farm.
But as time went on, he found that directors were always casting him in roles that required him to play an instrument, so he decided to make music his main focus.
Fenton got his first job as composer and musical director for a production of Twelfth Night at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1974.

Eight years later, he was nominated for an Oscar for his score for Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, on which he worked with Indian composer and instrumentalist Ravi Shankar to develop a score reflecting the country's musical traditions.
It was only his fourth attempt at film music, and he was still almost entirely self-taught.
Throughout the 1980s, he wrote the soundtrack for a number of TV series, including the Bafta-winning The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads.
He also wrote many well-known theme tunes, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme.

For 1987's Cry Freedom - the story of South African campaigner Steve Biko, who was brutally killed by police - he worked with South African jazz musician Jonas Gwangwa, earning two Oscar nominations for best original score and song.
Almost by accident, the title track featured Fenton singing a list of anti-apartheid activists imprisoned or killed by the South African government.
He'd initially recorded the lyrics as a guide for Gwangwa - but the musician decided to keep some of them intact "as a gesture of brotherhood".

"Then it got nominated for an Oscar, so I then found myself singing it on live television to about a billion people, which was not what I intended at all," Fenton later told Radio 4's Desert Island Discs.

After composing the score for the BBC's Trials of Life in 1990, Fenton went on to create the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.

Fenton's music perfectly complemented the stunning visuals of the ocean's depths and the polar ice caps, adding an emotional weight to the narrative, using the full might of the orchestra to evoke everything from wonder and awe to tension and suspense.
Following the success of the documentaries, Fenton created a show - The Blue Planet in Concert - which has been performed by leading orchestras in venues around the world.
Among his other well-known soundtracks were The Long Walk Home, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama, The Lady In The Van and Mrs Henderson Presents.
Fenton also scored more films for British director Ken Loach than any other composer.
Their 18 collaborations included Ladybird, Ladybird; I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival.

He also founded the Association of Professional Composers, which later merged with The Ivors Academy; and he is one of only a handful of musicians to receive the Academy's fellowship, alongside Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber, Sir Elton John, Kate Bush, Bruce Springsteen and George Michael.
In addition, Fenton was a visiting professor at the Royal College of Music and the University of Nottingham. He was made a CBE for services to music in 2023.
The composer often said that his musical career had been an accident, but nothing gave him greater joy than seeing his work come to life.

On his episode of Desert Island Discs, Fenton chose one of his own compositions - Reunion, from the soundtrack to the movie Accidental Hero - as it reminded him of watching pianist John Lowe play the melody in the studio.

"If I was sitting on a desert island and thinking about what a good time I'd had writing music, which I have, I want just one thing to remind me about the best part - which is the fact that you write something and then you're so surprised and thrilled at the way it's played," he told Sue Lawley.
"For a composer, that's the biggest kick you can get."

articles.title: Former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn sentenced to life in prison for wife's murder
articles.summary: A former music pastor in Ohio who appeared briefly on American Idol was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him last week of murdering his…

image.caption: Caleb Flynn is seen listening to a judge reading out a jury's verdict in an Ohio court on Sept. 29. The former American Idol contestant was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him of murdering his wife while he was having an affair. (The Assoc

blocks.text: World·New

A former music pastor in Ohio who appeared briefly on American Idol was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him last week of murdering his wife while he was having an affair.
Judge says Flynn showed no remorse for actions marked by 'deceit, manipulation and cruelty'
The judge said Caleb Flynn, 40, used his Christian faith to manipulate others and showed no remorse for actions marked by "layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty."

With tears rolling down his cheeks, Flynn apologized to his family just before being sentenced, starting with his two young daughters, who were home when he shot his wife in her sleep. He called their births the "greatest joy in this life."
Although he said he accepted responsibility for his words and decisions, Flynn remained adamant that he was innocent.
"As I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife," he said.
Did not testify in own defence

Prosecutors said Flynn staged a home invasion in February and claimed a burglar killed his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old schoolteacher and volleyball coach. In his 2013 appearance on American Idol, Flynn credited his wife with encouraging him to chase his dreams on the singing contest. He did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood.
During the trial, Flynn didn't testify on his own behalf, nor did anybody else.
Family members, including Ashley's parents, spoke in favour of the harsh sentence Monday, while saying they had forgiven Flynn because they didn't want her legacy to be hatred.

Her sister, Kayla Keyt, said Flynn's actions have scarred their entire church community, prompting children to run into their parents' bedrooms to make sure their fathers haven't killed their mothers.

As a family member read a statement written by his daughter Ava, Flynn sobbed uncontrollably as a pile of tissues grew on the defence table in front of him. At one point, it appeared he might fall over.

"Mommy was the perfect person," her statement said. "The absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to you to make you hate her so much?" In her statement, his daughter Alyssa said she wouldn't visit him in prison.
Wanted to leave marriage, jury told

During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their house in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying, "I choose you. I'm free. Actions will come tomorrow," prosecutors said.

During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her.

The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his attorney told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving around the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting.
The jury found him guilty of multiple counts, including murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
articles.summary: Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment.

blocks.text: "I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."

Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.

The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.

However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.

Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.

Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.

"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, told BBC Sinhala.
The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.

Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.

The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.

His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.

The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.
In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.

"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, President's Counsel, told BBC Sinhala.
Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.

"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."
In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.
In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.

"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.

Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.

There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.
Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: This couple was swatted 55 times in 2 years over a post about Norm Macdonald
articles.summary: A Milwaukee couple was awarded a $575,000 US settlement from the city after armed police officers showed up at their homes 55 times in two years responding to bogus reports of violent crimes.

image.caption: Niki Robinson, left, and Patrick Tomlinson have been awarded a $575,000 US settlement by the City Milwaukee after armed police officers came to their home 55 times in two years responding to bogus reports of violent crime. (Submitted by Patrick Tomlinson)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New
A Milwaukee couple was awarded a $575,000 US settlement from the city after armed police officers showed up at their homes 55 times in two years responding to bogus reports of violent crimes.
Patrick Tomlinson and Niki Robinson awarded $575K US settlement from City of Milwaukee
The first time heavily armed police officers showed up at Patrick Tomlinson's house, he was asleep in bed, naked.
It was 1 a.m. on July 25, 2022, and someone had reported a hostage situation at his house in Milwaukee, where he lives with his wife, Niki Robinson.
"All of a sudden there's people pounding on the door," Tomlinson told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
"I go outside to be pulled out of the house by eight or nine police officers [and] handcuffed on the front porch, which I can tell you is the least fun I've had handcuffed and naked in my life."

Tomlinson, a science fiction writer and comedian, hadn't committed a crime. He was the victim of "swatting," a harassment technique in which someone places a hoax call reporting a serious threat in order to send armed police to the target's home.

Over the course of the next two and a half years, Tomlinson and Robinson were swatted 55 times, despite repeatedly explaining their situation to the Milwaukee Police Department. They sued, and have been awarded a $575,000 US settlement from the City of Milwaukee.
LISTEN | Interview with 'swatting' victim Patrick Tomlinson:
As It Happens6:52This Milwaukee couple was swatted 55 times in 2 years
When asked for comment, Milwaukee police referred CBC to city attorney Evan Goyke, who did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

“While Niki and Patrick’s settlement provided closure and an acknowledgment of the violations of their rights, it is just as important that Milwaukee be more proactive looking forward," Jack Idlas, a lawyer for the couple, said in an emailed statement.

"The city has made no changes to policy and no officers have been disciplined for violating Niki and Patrick’s constitutional rights. That’s hard to believe after the taxpayers settled for over a half million dollars.
It started with a tweet
Tomlinson traces his troubles back to a social media post he made seven years ago about Canadian comedian Norm MacDonald.
In September 2018, he wrote on Twitter, now X: “Hot take: I’ve never found Norm Macdonald funny and was pretty sure all my comedy friends who did were either nuts or screwing with me."
After that, he says, he experienced years of online harassment, which is described in detail in an article in the Independent. That harassment, he says, eventually escalated into swatting.
"Our stalkers had specifically told us that they were going to begin swatting us…. We spoke to a dispatcher. We spoke with a desk sergeant. And both of them said there's nothing we can do," he said.
"Two weeks later, here I am, you know, on my front porch in the middle of the night, exposed to all my neighbours with shotguns and pistols and AR-15s pointed at my head."
Police were aware that Tomlinson's home was the target of swatting calls, according to internal memos and emails submitted as court evidence in the lawsuit.

On Aug. 3, 2022, one officer sent a memo to the acting police captain requesting the couple's home be marked as a "swatter house." The captain declined, saying it could cause a "complacency issue for responding officers.”
In bodycam footage from one incident, shared with CBC by Tomlinson's lawyers, an officer can be heard saying: "This guy keeps getting swatted."
Nevertheless, Tomlinson says, the police kept showing up, sometimes multiple times per day.

On one occasion, an officer entered his home without permission, according to an agreed statement of facts filed in connection with the lawsuit. On several occasions, officers searched the couple's home without a warrant.
Tomlinson says some of the officers responding to the hoax calls were "professional and sympathetic."
"Others, much less so," he said.

items: Trans Twitch star files human rights complaint against London, Ont., police after swatting arrest

blocks.text: It's been an exhausting ordeal for him and his wife, he said.

"Having each other there to support one another through this, emotionally and to know that we're not alone, without that, I don't think that either one of us individually would have been able to come out of this sane and intact," he said.
No charges or discipline
Nobody has been charged for the swatting calls, and none of the officers named in the lawsuit have been disciplined. The lawsuit settlement is not considered an admission of liability.

In his ruling, U.S. District Judge J.P. Stadtmueller determined that several police officers violated Tomlinson's and Robinson's constitutional rights by entering their home without permission and searching it without a warrant.

However, the judge granted those officers "qualified immunity," a legal doctrine that protects police and other government officials from prosecution or lawsuits for actions committed in the line of duty.
Most people don't realize that you don't have to be a celebrity or a politician to be targeted by this sort of thing.- Patrick Tomlinson, swatting victim
Tomlinson says he would like to see the officers involved disciplined, and for the police department to enact a detailed swatting policy.
In the meantime, he says, he and Robinson will keep speaking out.

"This is the only avenue, really, that we have to move the needle on this issue and to, you know, educate the public on this kind of harassment and stalking," he said. "Most people don't realize that you don't have to be a celebrity or a politician to be targeted by this sort of thing."
Interview with Patrick Tomlinson produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: Tesla's exclusion from Manitoba EV program 'incredibly unfair,' politically motivated, court hears
articles.summary: Who in the Manitoba government decided to exclude Tesla from the province's electric vehicle rebate program, and why, is still unclear following a court hearing on the decision, the company's lawyers…

image.caption: A 2022 file photo shows a driver charging a Tesla electric vehicle. The company argues its exclusion from Manitoba's EV rebate program was unfair. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

Who in the Manitoba government decided to exclude Tesla from the province's electric vehicle rebate program, and why, is still unclear following a court hearing on the decision, the company's lawyers argue.
Decision made as part of budget, can't be reviewed by court, province argues

Who in the Manitoba government decided to exclude Tesla from the province's electric vehicle rebate program, and why, is still unclear following a court hearing on the decision, the company's lawyers argued in court Monday.

Lawyers for Tesla Motors Canada asked a Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge to overturn the NDP government's decision to exclude the company from electric vehicle rebates in the province in 2025 and 2026.
That move was unreasonable and unfair, and lacked transparency, the lawyers argued.
Manitoba's EV rebate program, which rolled out in 2024, entitled Manitobans to a $4,000 rebate on some new electric or hybrid plug-in vehicles, or $2,500 on used vehicles.
But in its spring 2025 budget, released just after the trade war began between the U.S. and Canada, the provincial government cut Tesla out of the rebate program. Chinese EVs were also excluded.

Manitoba's cut followed similar moves in B.C. and in Ontario, where Tesla won a 2018 legal case against the provincial government over its exclusion. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island also announced Tesla exclusions from rebate programs the same month Manitoba did.

Tesla filed a judicial review application over the Manitoba exclusion earlier this year, naming the province, Manitoba Public Insurance and the ministers of finance, the environment and justice as respondents.
Manitoba budget targets Tesla, U.S. contractor in midst of trade war
The company argued its exclusion must be invalidated, since it's not clear which of the respondents made the decision or whether any of them were legally allowed to do so.
Michael Parrish, a lawyer for Tesla, called the province's decision to exclude Tesla "incredibly unfair."

A slim stack of documents provided by the province to show how it made the decision did not shed light on how a "still unidentified group of people" decided to exclude the company from the program, he told Justice Elissa Neville.
"What is at issue in this proceeding is the actual decision," he said. "We don't know why Tesla Canada was excluded, we don't know what information or documents were considered."

items: Tesla asks court to overturn exclusion from Manitoba EV rebate program

blocks.text: Tesla says it was not consulted before the exclusion and received no rationale from the province, aside from reading media reports that the decision was "made in order to be 'elbows up' in relation to the United States of America," the application says.

In court Monday, Parrish pointed to comments made by Premier Wab Kinew shortly after the company threatened legal action last May, in which the premier said Tesla CEO Elon Musk — a onetime ally of the U.S. president — should "get Donald Trump to stop the tariffs, and then we can talk about the EV rebate."
Based on those comments, Parrish argued that Tesla Canada was excluded from the EV rebate for "seemingly political reasons."
Tesla also argued the exclusion runs counter to the rebate program's objectives of making EVs more affordable for Manitobans.
'Budgetary decision': province
Joseph Langan, a lawyer for the Manitoba government, said the decision to exclude Tesla was made as part of the provincial budget and is therefore unreviewable by the courts.
"This doesn't belong in a judicial review. This is a policy decision. This is a budgetary decision," he said.
"This was ultimately a funding decision ... of the government."
Parrish argued that a government decision made for an improper purpose will always be under the court's purview.
Langan also said the slim stack of documents that informed the province's decision was all the government provided.

"We went to the people who decide what the budget will be, and we said, 'We need the decision on excluding Tesla vehicles,' and the documents provided are what's before you now, and you can see that there's very little there," he said.
"Sometimes there is little record."
Justice Neville reserved her decision until a later date.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ozten Shebahkeget is a member of Northwest Angle 33 First Nation, born and raised in Winnipeg. She started writing for CBC Manitoba during the first Pathways program in 2022. She holds a master's degree in writing from the University of Saskatchewan.
