articles.title: New York state declares measles disaster emergency
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration ​by a U.S. state since cases began surging in ​2025. New York has…

image.caption: A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center in New Hyde Park, N.Y., in March 2025. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration ​by a U.S. state since cases began surging in ​2025. New York has reported 108 measles ‌cases so far this year, with seven cases in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.
New York reported 108 measles ‌cases so far this year, with 7 cases in New York City, 101 elsewhere in state
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration ​by a U.S. state since cases began surging in ​2025.
The state also expanded the pool of health professionals allowed to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines as cases rise in rural communities.
"No one ​should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul ⁠said in a ⁠statement.

New York has reported 108 measles ‌cases this year through Oct. 3, including 92 since July 15 in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order.

Seven of the cases are in New York ⁠City and 101 are elsewhere in the state, the governor's office said. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.
Trump signs executive order calling to reduce childhood vaccinations
Neighbouring ‌Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak, with 977 cases and five deaths as of Oct. 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said.
Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state's total had ​passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.

items: Bangladesh in grips of world's worst measles outbreak, with 1,000 dead in last 6 months

blocks.text: The U.S. is ⁠having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, ⁠according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The order allows registered nurses ⁠to ⁠order tests for suspected measles and ​pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations ​to be reported ⁠to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults' consent for such reporting.
Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through Nov. 4.

articles.title: Coalition set to unveil dramatically deeper cuts to overseas migration as it fends off One Nation’s rise
articles.summary:
Sources say the opposition’s target will be below Labor’s but won’t match One Nation’s goal to limit net arrivals to 130,000

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Coalition is expected to reveal deep cuts to immigration today which the party says would maintain working holidaymaker places and prioritise skills as part of attempts to dent growing support for One Nation.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, is expected to unveil the Coalition’s policy on Tuesday, after signoff from Liberal and National MPs in a special party room meeting due to convene this morning.

Liberal sources told Guardian Australia the Coalition’s target for net overseas migration (Nom) would be significantly below Labor’s new target, but not cut as much as One Nation, which wants to limit net arrivals to 130,000 people annually, after a brief initial period of net negative migration.

The Nine newspapers reported the Coalition would initially drop net migration to around 100,000 in the first year after the election before it rose again to a figure between One Nation’s 130,000 and Labor’s target of 225,000.
As previously announced by Taylor, the number of new arrivals will be linked to housing completions in Australia.

One Nation announced last month it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.
The Coalition’s plan is likely to contain the largest cuts in the first year, in an effort to make an immediate impact on Nom.
Foreign students and people overstaying their visas will be part of the Coalition’s crackdown, as well as measures to remove individuals in the country without a legal pathway to stay.
Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependants or family members of the primary applicant.
Labor’s plan, outlined by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, will see a series of policy changes to bring Nom down to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28.
Most students will not be allowed to bring family members, and so-called visa hopping would be banned, limiting the changes students can make to their enrolment.

Nationals MPs have warned Labor’s plans to limit the number of working holidaymakers staying a second and third year in Australia would badly hurt regional industries including fruit picking, and have pushed for carve outs.
after newsletter promotion

Labor plans a ballot for backpackers wanting to stay beyond the initial first year, a measure designed to cut the number of temporary workers in the country. But regional hospitality and agriculture businesses have lobbied the Coalition to avoid cuts to its workforce.

Taylor is under pressure to stop and reverse an exodus of support to One Nation, as the party surpasses the Coalition and Labor in some opinion polls and its leader Pauline Hanson increasingly sets the terms for political and policy debate on immigration.
Liberal MP Andrew Wallace confirmed the plan had been modelled to test its effect on the Australian economy.
“You can’t just slash immigration altogether,” he told Channel Nine.
“The Coalition’s plan on migration will be very, very carefully targeted towards ensuring that we have the right number of people coming into the country, but also the right skills.
“We’ve got to ensure that our farmers and our key industries have the right skills to be able to keep the country moving, and that’s what we’ll be focused on.”
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who defected from the Nationals last year, claimed credit for the Coalition plan on Tuesday.
“I congratulate the Coalition for basically coming up with our policy. There’s a bit of a nuance in there, but you know what? It shows an endorsement of where One Nation is off to,” he said.

articles.title: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
articles.summary: France prepares for a day of protests in support of students who’ve been demanding more investment in education.

blocks.text: France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education.
It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested.
One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week.

France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete".
The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement".
Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest.

The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.

The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers.
The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry, external.
Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors.

The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner".
While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand.
The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response.

"This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Meanwhile Mélenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations".

The left-wing mayor of Marseille, Benoît Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.

articles.title: ICC unseals Taliban leaders' warrants over persecuting women
articles.summary: The court gave more details on the warrants for four Taliban leaders accused of the crime against humanity of gender persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community. The Islamist group rejected…

image.caption: The Taliban has significantly restricted several rights of women and girls since taking power [FILE: May 23, 2023]Image: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Criminal Court (ICC) disclosed on Monday more details about the arrest warrants against two Taliban leaders, while also issuing two more arrest warrants.
The four Taliban leaders are accused of crimes against humanity through the persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community in Afghanistan since taking power in 2021.

According to the court, warrants were issued in July and September of last year against Hibatullah Akhundzada , the Taliban's Supreme Leader, as well as against Abdul Hakim Haqqani, who heads the country's Supreme Court.
The other two warrants were issued against Education Minister Habibullah Agha and Minister of Higher Education Neda Mohammad Nadim.

The four are charged with persecution on grounds of gender of "girls, women and other persons nonconforming with the Taliban's policy on gender, gender identity or expression; and on political grounds against persons perceived as 'allies of girls and women,'" according to the court.

blocks.caption: An arrest warrant was issued against Taliban Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhundzada [FILE: Aug 14, 2023]Image: WAKIL KOHSAR/AFP

blocks.text: What does the ICC accuse the 4 Taliban leaders of?

The judges who issued the warrants said that the four implemented policies that saw "severe violations of fundamental rights and freedoms of the civilian population of Afghanistan, in connection with conducts of murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance."

The Taliban "specifically targeted girls and women by reason of their gender," the judges added, also mentioning persecution against people due to "certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity."
The ICC has no jurisdiction to execute the warrants. Still, the move is considered a form of pressure on the Afghan ruling authority.
The Taliban have taken a wide range of measures to restrict women's access to jobs and education beyond sixth grade, as well as barring them from most public spaces.
Women are also obligated to cover their whole bodies apart from their eyes upon leaving home, with a male relative having to accompany them on long trips.
Taliban rejects ICC's warrants
Afghanistan's government spokesperson said the country does not recognize the court's authority.
"We are bound by the rulings of Islamic Sharia and its courts, not by intelligence entities or so-called courts." chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The Taliban has returned to rule over Afghanistan since August 2021Image: Javid Ashna/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: A request for warrants for Akhundzada and Haqqani made last year by former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan argued that "Afghan women and girls as well as the LGBTQI+ community are facing an unprecedented, unconscionable and ongoing persecution by the Taliban.”
The UN Human Rights Council has called on the Taliban to drop its "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan."
Human rights groups have been calling for the international community to do more against the Taliban's gender-based policies in Afghanistan.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro rides right-wing wave to win first round of Brazil election
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro's success could be the latest example of a resurgence of right-wing support in Latin America.

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro's success in Brazil's presidential election is being hailed as the result of a "blue wave" - the latest example of a resurgence of right-wing support sweeping Latin America.

But despite missing an outright majority – meaning there will be a second round later this month – the unexpectedly clear first round victory leaves his left-wing opponent needing an unprecedented result to retain the presidency.
Senator Bolsonaro is the eldest son of ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, who became known as the "Trump of the Tropics" due to his ideological alignment with the US president.
The younger Bolsonaro is 45 years old and is part of the-right wing political dynasty initiated by his father.
He had never before run for the presidency and surprised observers by finishing ahead of the 80-year-old president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, of the Workers' Party.
All polls had indicated a close race, with Lula and Bolsonaro statistically tied. But that was not what happened on Sunday. Flávio obtained 56.1 million votes, while Lula received 53.8 million.
Part of Bolsonaro's success at the ballot box may be related less to his popularity and more to the numbers of people rejecting Lula.

Bolsonaro has presented himself as a dynamic young politician connected to the demands of younger voters, including concerns about rising crime rates in a country that records more than 40,000 homicides annually.
But polling groups such as Datafolha, one of Brazil's most respected institutes, suggest that this election has been a battle of rejection rates.
Its most recent survey suggested that, on the eve of the election, both candidates had the same rejection rate with voters: 45%.
The problem for Lula, however, appeared to be worse.
One poll showed that 49% disapproved of his government, while the approval rate stood at 48%.
Analysts had been saying that never before in Brazilian history had a president managed to seek re-election with such a high disapproval rate.

Voter dissatisfaction with Lula's government shows that the left-wing leader is facing a paradox. The official unemployment rate is at its lowest level in history, around 5.3%. Average income is also at its highest level since records began.
Despite the economy's apparent solid performance, Brazilians have shown considerable dissatisfaction with their current living conditions.
In an attempt to address this issue, Lula increased by 15% the value of Bolsa Família, the government's main social welfare program.
He also banned online gambling, which was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction.
A second factor behind Flávio Bolsonaro's success is the way he positioned himself in relation to the Brazilian Supreme Court.
He spent much of his campaign criticising the court's actions, in way similar way to his father when he was president.

Bolsonaro criticised the conviction of his father by the same court for an attempted coup d'état in 2023, when thousands of people invaded the buildings of the three branches of government in Brasília. It was compared to the 6 January Capitol Hill attack in 2021 in Washington DC.

Bolsonaro senior's 27-year prison sentence in 2025 was heavily criticised by the right and remained controversial, particularly because of the role played by Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case and was close to Lula.

Flávio Bolsonaro was also able to use another controversy involving Moraes to his political advantage: the Banco Master corruption scandal involving the Brazilian banker Daniel Vorcaro, who was arrested in March.
Vorcaro is alleged to have orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiling senior figures across the political spectrum.
Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing.
Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.
A second aspect of Flávio Bolsonaro's victory goes beyond the presidential election.

In the Senate, the Liberal Party, led by the Bolsonaros, jumped from 15 seats to 28. The strength of the Bolsonaro family can be seen by the fact that the ex-president's wife, Michelle, and another son, Carlos, were both elected for the Senate.
Lula faces an extremely difficult task. Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.
Political analyst Dora Kramer, writing for Folha de S Paulo, argues that both Lula and Flávio will have to focus their efforts on independent voters.
Brazilians like to say that politics in their country is so unstable that not even the past is predictable. At this point, a comeback by Lula seems more distant, though not impossible.

In any case, even if he succeeds in achieving an unprecedented reversal against Flávio Bolsonaro, one thing is certain: the Bolsonarist right has consolidated itself as an unavoidable political force.

articles.title: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.summary: The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed the B1 bombers from the base in England back to their home stations in America.

blocks.text: Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
Washington, he added, "actually knows the people that made the threat", he but did not confirm who.

The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairfield remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.

One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
"Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.
Trump's comments, and those of Vice-President JD Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.

He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.

Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

articles.title: US 'watching closely' after plague researcher dies in Russia, Rubio says
articles.summary: The US says it is monitoring the case of a lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.

blocks.text: The US says it is closely monitoring the case of a Russian lab technician who died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was concern the incident could have led to the spread of pneumonic plague, but that there was no cause for alarm.
Announcing the cause of death as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology", Irkutsk's governor said that "no micro-organisms" linked to the woman's work had been found "in her biological samples".

Unconfirmed reports had suggested the woman fell ill either after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen or following a field trip to a region where plague is found naturally among wild rodents.

No other cases of staff from the plague institute seeking medical attention since her death had been reported, Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said, quoting Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor.
The watchdog said a biological safety team had inspected the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk and found no emergency situation there.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged people not to "listen to various rumours" but "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements" instead.
Russian media reported last week that nearly 200 people known to have had contact with the dead woman were under medical observation as a precaution.

Asked by a reporter for an "update on the suspected plague case in Russia", Rubio said: "It seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected and there's concern that that, you know, could have spread, at least internally - you've seen them do quarantine of this and that nature.

"If something like that gets out, it can quickly spread. So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and the cause to just keep an eye on it and we're doing that."
The woman who died, whose first name was given by Russian media as Daria and who was in her late twenties, had recently visited the Buryatia region on the border with Mongolia.

The plague bacterium or Yersinia pestis, external, which killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death, is found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, external was founded just over 100 years ago.

Dr Simon Clarke, an associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the pneumonic version of Yersinia pestis was nearly always fatal if left untreated, but could be overcome with antibiotics.
"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."
Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible.
"Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.

articles.title: Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen
articles.summary:
Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory

Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several…

blocks.text: Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.

The officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.
The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by the Houthis.

However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.

Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said that Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.
He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.

The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.

Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.

Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.

Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Australia's migrant policy offers lessons for EU and US
articles.summary: Australia has used offshore processing centers to deter asylum seekers for more than two decades. As the EU and US pursue similar third-country arrangements, Australia's experience highlights the…

image.caption: There have been allegations of human rights abuses and neglect in Australia's offshore migration centersImage: Rick Rycroft/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nations that send asylum seekers to third countries for offshore processing and holding could spend billions, only to face accusations of human rights abuses and financial mismanagement, as in Australia.

The European Union (EU) has nevertheless been considering the idea, and the United States (US) has already made similar third-country deals, but Australia has been processing or relocating people outside the country where they seek protection for more than two decades.

Former Australian Prime Minister John Howard introduced the so-called "Pacific Solution" in 2001, targeting immigrants who arrived by boat, and establishing Australian migration processing centers with the help from governments in Papua New Guinea (PNG) and the tiny island nation of Nauru .
Thousands sent to islands under Australia's 'Pacific Solution'

Center-left and center-right governments described the policy as a deterrent, saying people were less likely to attempt dangerous ocean crossings or pay smugglers if arriving by boat did not provide a route to Australia. In his 2001 election policy speech, Howard said the famous line, frequently quoted since: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."
In 2008, a newly elected Labor Party government phased out the practice, saying it was a cynical, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful exercise.

But faced with more deaths at sea, a Labor government under Prime Minister Julia Gillard started sending maritime arrivals to Nauru and Manus again in 2012, after an expert panel recommended reopening the centers.
"I'm not going to play politics or look at political scoreboards when too many lives have been lost," Gillard said at the time.
Between 2013 and 2014, the number of people transferred offshore peaked to more than 3,000.

Journalists have been mostly barred from the centers on Nauru and Manus Island. Graham Thom, Advocacy Coordinator for the Refugee Council of Australia (RCOA), told DW that this lack of access and independent oversight meant many Australians accepted the narrative that the policy was working.

blocks.caption: Australia has been sending aslyum seekers who arrive by boat to Nauru for more than 20 yearsImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: EU considers offshore arrangements

People without a legal right to remain in the EU could face deportation to third countries as soon as 2027, with Rwanda and Uzbekistan reportedly under consideration as third-party countries, as well as Uganda.
The European Parliament in June approved new rules that would pave the way for so-called "return hubs" outside the EU's borders.
Denmark's Minister for Immigration and Integration, Morten Bodskov, told reporters last month the hubs would not be detention and deportation centers.
"We are not talking about camps," Bodskov said, describing the scheme instead as "a new chance to have a life in a partner country."

Denmark, alongside Germany, Austria, Greece, and the Netherlands, known collectively as the Group of Five, said in September they had agreed on steps towards a deal with a non-EU country, without naming it.
The group was to speak with the United Nations (UN) body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency about their next steps.
The proposal allows for harsh penalties for those who refuse to be removed to the hubs, including detention for up to 30 months pending deportation from the EU and entry bans.
US already has a third country migration scheme

The US government has already made deals with at least 30 third countries in Africa and Latin America. In June, Amnesty International said some agreements had been revealed through the US Freedom of Information Act, while others "remain secret."

The US Supreme Court ruled late last month that the second Trump administration could resume deportations under the third-country scheme, after a US appeals court ruled that immigrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture.

The first deportations from the US under the third-country removal scheme were of immigrants convicted of crimes, but more recently, foreign nationals not accused of any crime have also been deported.
Trump deportees to Cameroon face life of uncertainty
Accusations of human rights abuse
Asylum seekers and human rights advocates have repeatedly alleged human rights abuses in Australia's offshore migration processing program, with Thom describing the policy as a "medieval idea."
A group of asylum seekers formerly detained on Manus Island reached a AU$70 million (€43.47 million/$48.47 million) settlement in 2017 after filing charges for abuse and unlawful detention.

In February, an Australian Senate inquiry heard first-hand witness accounts of neglect, untreated health conditions, and serious concerns for the safety and dignity of camps inhabitants — especially of women being kept on Nauru. Prior to the hearing, 73 UN member states had publicly raised concerns about Australia's migration policies.

blocks.caption: Australia and Nauru have agreed on a billion-dollar deal for certain convicted foreign nationals to be deported to the Pacific Island nationImage: Dominic Giannini/AAP Image via AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil, China, Finland, Germany, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey called for an end to offshore processing of asylum claims.

Australia has yet to officially comment on the recommendations, but successive governments have said offshore processing helps deter dangerous boat journeys, with former Prime Minister Tony Abbott describing the policy during his term as "decent, humane and compassionate."

The effect of offshore processing is difficult to isolate from other policy measures, especially the practice of turning back asylum boats. This "turnback" policy was introduced and reintroduced under conservative governments in 2001 and 2013 respectively, but with inconsistent data on incidents.

As in the US, offshore migration processing for Australia has expanded beyond its original scope, with Nauru recently agreeing to accept convicted foreign nationals from Australia who can't legally be returned to their countries of origin, at a cost of AU$2.5 billion over the next 30 years. Australia had already spent more than AU$13 billion on offshore detention since 2012.

Measuring the success of Australia's model is difficult, but its significant long-term costs and legal and human rights concerns may serve as a warning for other countries considering similar policies.

articles.title: Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
articles.summary: European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’
articles.byline: Aletha Adu, Peter Walker and Deborah Cole

blocks.text: The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens.
The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right of Israel to exist.
The binding policy motion passed in a vote at the Greens’ conference in Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.

The policy says Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”.

The European Green party, which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this.

The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the German Greens, said the policy ‘runs counter to what the European Green party stands for’. Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/M Behrens/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Felix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”.
“It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for in Germany, and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added.

Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”.
Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism.
The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly.

blocks.caption: Ellie Chowns, who opposed the motion, said the party’s policymaking ‘urgently needs to be modernised’. Photograph: Ellie & Adrian 2025/PA

blocks.text: Policy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.
Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”.

“As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.”
Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.”
One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel.

They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.”

Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking.
They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership.

blocks.caption: The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, who missed the vote himself, earlier addressed the conference alongside the MPs Hannah Spencer, left, and Siân Berry, right. Berry opposed the motion.  Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian

blocks.text: Another senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character.

Daniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion.

“Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.”

In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.”

He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”

articles.title: Avengers: Endgame once again beats Avatar as highest-grossing movie of all time
articles.summary: Marvel's Avengers: Endgame has recaptured its title as the highest-grossing movie of all time this weekend (not accounting for inflation). It overtook James Cameron's biggest release with a gross of…

image.caption: A scene from Marvel's Avengers: Endgame is shown. The film has once again become the highest-earning movie. (Marvel Studios)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Marvel's Avengers: Endgame has recaptured its title as the highest-grossing movie of all time this weekend (not accounting for inflation). It overtook James Cameron's biggest release with a gross of $2.9255 billion US, narrowly superseding Avatar's $2.9237 billion US.
Re-release of MCU superhero team-up surged to historic No. 1 at the global box office this weekend

Marvel's Avengers: Endgame recaptured its title this weekend as the highest-grossing movie of all time (not accounting for inflation). With a gross of $2.9255 billion US, the Disney title narrowly superseded James Cameron's biggest release, Avatar, at $2.9237 billion US.

The shift follows Endgame's recent re-release in theatres, and represents the second time it has overtaken Avatar at the box office. Hitting theatres late last month with four additional minutes, the slightly recut version of Marvel's superhero super-collage debuted to $86 million US at the global box office ($26 million US domestic), according to parent company Disney.

The film was re-released as an anticipatory tee-up to Avengers: Doomsday, the next in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's cycle of big-budget team-up films. Due to release Dec. 18, that movie will reintroduce a number of familiar faces, including stars like Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans.

It is a chance for the MCU to recapture the cultural zeitgeist after disappointing recent entries — like Thunderbolts* and Captain America: Brave New World — whose new leading characters failed to capture audience interest.

Among re-releases, only 1997's Star Wars: A New Hope ($35.9 million US) and 2011's The Lion King ($30.2 million US) have opened higher than Endgame in domestic cinemas. That release set its own record in 2019 — it was then that the Marvel film's total gross overtook Avatar, the intergalactic film about war between Na'vi and humans, shortly after its release.

It was a historic achievement; Cameron had actually individually held the record since 1998, when Titanic became the all-time highest-grossing film. While the ocean-liner epic reached its gross of $1.84 billion US via markedly lower ticket prices, Avatar's ascendance was still shocking, surging to the top spot in 2010 after just 39 days in theatres.
But when Endgame finally broke his streak in 2019, Cameron did not appear to be a sore loser.

“Oel ngati kameie,” the Canadian New Zealand director shared on X (then Twitter) at the time, using a phrase from his film's fictional language. “I see you, Marvel. Congratulations to Avengers: Endgame on becoming the new box-office king.”

But after a 2021 re-release in China, Cameron's Avatar beat Marvel once again, catapulting to a gross of over $2.8 billion US. Endgame directors Joe and Anthony Russo then took to social media to congratulate Cameron, writing in a post, “Passing the gauntlet back to you.”
An unpredictable box office

The latest record flip-flop comes at a uniquely unpredictable time for the box office. Hollywood had its best summer on record this year, posting $4.76 billion US in domestic ticket sales, according to analytics firm Rentrak.

items: Digger is poised to be one of the biggest box-office flops of the year
Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars bombs at the box office. Here's what that tells us about what audiences want

blocks.text: But it came along with a slew of poor performers, like Steven Spielberg's return to sci-fi filmmaking, Disclosure Day, and the Spielberg-style nostalgia dinosaur flick The End of Oak Street, which similarly failed to pull audiences in despite strong reviews and famous faces like Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor.

Then the Jacob Elordi-led apocalypse film The Dog Stars let down 20th Century Studios, bombing with roughly $8 million US domestic in its opening weekend against a reported $80-million US production budget. Tom Cruise's Digger saw perhaps the A-lister's biggest flop of his career, opening with a shocking $8 million US domestically against a reported budget of between $125 million US to $180 million US.
That is on top of a dismal year for studio Warner Bros., none of whose offerings surpassed $100 million US in the domestic box office.

Meanwhile, strange genre fare — like Obsession, Resident Evil and Backrooms — has pulled in strong numbers, suggesting audiences are more than ever interested in the surprising and specific over the established franchise.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surge
articles.summary:
Experts say strength of evangelical church and perception that Lula is too old also helped propel Jair Bolsonaro’s son to first-round election win

On Sunday night, as the scale of the…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: On Sunday night, as the scale of the far-right triumph in Brazil sank in, an adapted football chant rang out in one of Rio’s most leftwing areas.

“Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa!” crestfallen progressives bellowed while drowning their sorrows after witnessing an excruciating election setback for their leader, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

But the scale of the challenge facing the veteran leftist looks immense after Flávio Bolsonaro’s shock first-round win, which analysts attribute to a complex lattice of social, political and religious phenomena.

“Flávio Bolsonaro’s result shows that Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” said Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo. “His father [Jair Bolsonaro] was convicted and jailed for attempting a coup d’état [in 2022-23] yet despite this, his allies won elections across the country, and his son is the frontrunner in the second round of the presidential election.”
Among the main drivers behind Bolsonaro’s strong showing:

items: 1. The evangelical churchBrazil’s evangelical church has expanded dramatically since the 1980s, with evangelical Christians now making up nearly a third of the population.Many evangelical voters – often influenced by church leaders – have thrown their weight behind the radical populist movement built by Jair Bolsonaro, and now spearheaded by his evangelical eldest son. As president from 2018 to 2022, Bolsonaro’s ultra-conservative policies helped him cement a lasting alliance with powerful megachurch leaders such as the televangelist Silas Malafaia.“This religious machine … was put at the service of Bolsonarismo: starting with these pastors who have millions of followers on social media, who buy airtime on TV, who lead churches with millions of members, and who turned themselves into canvassers for the Bolsonaro family,” said Mello Franco.

2. Urban violenceMello Franco believed urban violence was another factor that had turbocharged the “far-right windstorm” sweeping Brazil.Rightwing populists such as the pro-gun Bolsonaros were offering voters “misguided but easy-to-understand solutions” to high crime rates, such as increased police violence, mass incarceration and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. “This appeals to an electorate that is scared of violence and crime,” Mello Franco said.The leading light of such “security populism” in Latin America is El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, who has jailed thousands of people, often without due process, in his successful bid to cut murder rates. Mello Franco said El Salvador’s “proto-dictator” and his supposedly “magic solutions” had been held up as an inspiration by Bolsonarista politicians during the 2026 campaign.Such hardline proposals have also been boosted by Donald Trump’s decision to designate Brazil’s two biggest crime groups, Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s PCC, as foreign terrorist organizations. On the campaign trail, Bolsonaro and his allies have vowed to “neutralize narco-terrorists” and chemically castrate rapists – promises that appear to have won over many violence-weary voters.

3. Lula’s campaignAnalysts say Lula’s failure to focus on day-to-day issues such as crime may have hurt his prospects.The leftwing veteran spent much of the campaign vowing to defend Brazil’s sovereignty from Donald Trump’s “colonial” designs and protect its rare earth reserves. “Meanwhile, what voters wanted were solutions to more immediate problems such as bank debts, the cost of food, and insecurity,” Mello Franco said.During one recent rally in suburban Rio, some Lula supporters visibly zoned out as the president waxed lyrical about critical minerals and artificial intelligence.Political analyst Thomas Traumann, who was spokesperson for the former leftwing president Dilma Rousseff, believed Lula’s third administration had ignored a large chunk of society that was unsatisfied over economic issues or because of controversies involving the supreme court.“The government treated any kind of criticism … as a display of fascism – which undoubtedly exists in Brazil – and elitism, which also exists,” he said. “But what also exists is a group of voters who expected more from the government and who are neither fascists, nor elitists. They are simply people who didn’t like the government and decided to punish it.”

4. A Brazilian Biden?Some critics have also pointed to Lula’s age as his achilles heel and blame him for failing to produce an obvious successor. He will turn 81 two days after the election’s 25 October second round. One recent story in the Economist called Lula “a doddering leftie” and compared him to the “geriatric leader” Joe Biden, who was forced to abandon his 2024 re-election campaign after a disastrous debate performance against Trump.Traumann called questions over Lula’s physical or mental state “ridiculous”. “When you see him speak, you can tell it’s not about this,” he said of the gym-going octogenarian.Mello Franco agreed: “Unlike Biden, Lula has at no point shown any kind of physical frailty or cognitive impairment. I don’t think this was an issue.”But Traumann did see one parallel with the former US president: like Biden, Lula was stubborn, had not listened enough to others, and appeared to have thought decent economic indicators were enough to ensure re-election. “This disconnection from reality reminds me of Biden,” he said, attributing it to “the stubbornness of age”.From the start of the campaign, Lula seemed to believe “the election was in the bag”.“And it wasn’t,” Traumann said.

5. The global far rightMany observers saw Sunday’s rightwing victory as another chapter in the global advance of the social media-savvy far right.“We’re seeing this revolution in many other parts of the world. We’re seeing this in the US, we’re seeing it in parts of Latin America, we’re see this in a different way in Europe,” said Miguel Lagos, a political scientist.Lagos believed that in Brazil, the movement was driven by a deep “rage against the classical political elites” including journalists, traditional politicians and intellectuals.Jair Bolsonaro and his son Flávio are career politicians. Between them, they have spent half a century working in Rio’s state legislature or the Brazilian congress. Even so, father and son have managed to portray themselves as Trump-style anti-establishment outsiders who have come to drain a swamp of which they, too, are part.Mello Franco believed Bolsonaro was now the favourite to become president. “But I don’t think the contest is over,” he cautioned. “Brazil is always showing us that plot twists aren’t just possible – they’re practically part of the landscape.”

articles.title: Crown says DNA evidence helped ID man now on trial for decades-old sex assaults against children
articles.summary: Prosecutors told a jury in Brampton, Ont., on Monday, how DNA evidence had linked three brutal attacks against children in the 1990s to Richard Neil, now 67 and on trial for charges including…

image.caption: Richard Neil, on trial in Brampton, Ont., for a series of sex assaults against children in the 1990s, has pleaded not guilty to the 17 charges he's facing including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug. (Peel Regional Police)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Prosecutors told a jury in Brampton, Ont., on Monday, how DNA evidence had linked three brutal attacks against children in the 1990s to Richard Neil, now 67 and on trial for charges including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.
Richard Neil on trial for series of attacks in southern Ontario
WARNING: This story contains details of sexual assaults against children.
For three decades, the brutal cold case confounded police.
An unidentified attacker had violently tied up three children as young as eight in southern Ontario parks between 1992 and 1995. He sexually assaulted each of them and got away every time.
At a court in Brampton, Ont., on Monday, prosecutors told a jury how DNA evidence had finally linked each attack to Richard Neil, now 67.
As Neil's trial got underway, Crown attorney Shazin Karim went into graphic detail about the attacks — involving urination and anal penetration — and how they were reported to police at the time.
The victims were an eight-year-old boy, a 10-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl, Karim said.
"They were children," she said, underlining to the jury some of the evidence "may be difficult to hear."
Neil has pleaded not guilty to the 17 charges he's facing, including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.
Karim told the jurors investigators had first identified him as a suspect in recent years thanks to genetic genealogy analysis conducted in the U.S.
The investigative technique — which involves comparing crime scene DNA to genetic data voluntarily submitted to direct-to-consumer genealogical services — was unavailable to police in the 1990s.
Karim said police later uncovered further evidence that positively identified Neil as the assailant.
According to the Crown's opening statement to the jury, Neil's fingerprints matched those lifted by police from a bag and a bottle carried by the attacker all those years ago.
His DNA also matched samples recovered from each of the three crime scenes — Brampton's Norton Place Park, Idlewood Park in Kitchener and Wildwood Park in Oakville — the Crown said.
Neil wore a dark suit jacket and white buttoned shirt in the courtroom, seated next to his lawyer Leo Adler. The accused appeared to glance over at jurors during Karim's opening statement.

According to an indictment filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Neil is also accused of making "a video tape recording constituting child pornography" on the date of the Oakville attack on the girl.
The victims' identities are covered by a publication ban.
Karim told the jury employment records show Neil worked at Canada Post in Waterloo at the time of the assault in neighbouring Kitchener in 1992.
What's more, the prosecutor said when police seized Neil's electronic devices following his arrest in 2024, they found photos and videos pointing to an "interest" in urine drinking.
Karim said the victims' accounts of what happened is not contested. But she said the defence disputes the allegation that Neil was the assailant.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
articles.summary:
Police and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-Hammami

Investigators believe that the co-pilot who tried to take control…
articles.byline: Jason Burke in London and Stephanie Kirchgaessner in Washington

blocks.text: Investigators believe that the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.

The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe.

Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.

Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.

Israeli media have quoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near ⁠Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

blocks.caption: Capt Smit Machchhar was visited on Sunday in hospital in the UAE by Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, the crown prince of Dubai. Photograph: Hamdan bin Mohammed/X/Reuters

blocks.text: The investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are probing reports that the co-pilot studied in both about 10 years ago.

Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, but left the airline after being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.

Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.
A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.
Netanyahu has claimed Hammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.

blocks.caption: FlyDubai conducted checks on Hammami for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said. Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.

An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.

“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.

“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, the co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.
Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.
Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.

The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.
Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.

“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”

articles.title: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats after closing of East Jerusalem consulate
articles.summary:
Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements

The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British…

blocks.text: The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.

This could means as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel.

The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.

Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade with goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.

The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.

The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.
An Israeli diplomatic sources said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.
“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”

The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.

It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence as yet that the UK decision has yet played very big in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats may make the issue more high profile.

The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Milband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s, government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Israel disputes this.
after newsletter promotion

Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.
France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.

articles.title: Denmark: Data of millions compromised in hack
articles.summary: The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised.

image.caption: The hacker has not yet been apprehended [FILE: March 12, 2024]Image: Loïc Déquier/PHOTOPQR/SUD OUEST/picture alliance

blocks.text: Denmark's national registry was hacked in an incident the authorities described as "extremely serious."

Hackers secured access to personal information on millions of people, the country's digital affairs ministry said on Monday. The compromised information included names, addresses and social security numbers, known in Denmark as national registry numbers.

The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised. This figure exceeds Denmark's population size because it includes people who have already died or emigrated, the Danish authorities said in a statement.

The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The hackers have not yet been identified. The means they used to gain access has since been cut off.
The ministry said it was first alerted to an "anomaly" in the system "during September."
Information of deceased, emigrated people included

Denmark has a population of roughly six million people. However, its national registry includes information of eleven million people, which includes the data of those deceased or people who have moved abroad and don't live in Denmark anymore.
Christina Egelund, Denmark's digital affairs minister, said the incident's full extent will investigated by the authorities.
"This is an extremely serious incident," Egelund said. "We are in the process of tracking the exact extent of this incident with all those affected."

blocks.caption: Minister Christina Egelund called the breach 'very serious' [FILE: May 3, 2024]Image: Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/IMAGO

blocks.text: Danish news agency Ritzau reported that the register includes information on church membership, details of legal incapacitation and restrictions on legal capacity.
